metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: for young people around the world. And now, here's my conversation with Markus Hutter. Do you think

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: of the universe as a computer or maybe an information processing system? Let's go with a big question first.

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: Okay, with a big question first. I think it's a very interesting hypothesis or idea, and I have a background in physics,

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: so I know a little bit about physical theories, the Standard Model of Particle Physics and General

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: Relativity Theory, and they are amazing and describe virtually everything in the universe,

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: and they're all, in a sense, computable theories. I mean, they're very hard to compute,

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: and it's very elegant, simple theories which describe virtually everything in the universe.

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: So there's a strong indication that somehow the universe is computable, but it's a plausible hypothesis.

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: So what do you think, just like you said, General Relativity, Quantum Field Theory, what do you think

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: that the laws of physics are so nice and beautiful and simple and compressible? Do you think our

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: universe was designed, is naturally this way? Are we just focusing on the parts that are especially

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: compressible? Are human minds just enjoy something about that simplicity, and in fact, there's other

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: things that are not so compressible? No, I strongly believe, and I'm pretty convinced,

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: that the universe is inherently beautiful, elegant, and simple, and described by these equations,

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: and we're not just picking that. I mean, if there were some phenomena which cannot be neatly described,

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: scientists would try that, right? And there's biology which is more messy,

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: but we understand that it's an emergent phenomena, and it's complex systems, but they still follow

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: the same rules of quantum and electrodynamics. All of chemistry follows that, and we know that.

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: I mean, we cannot compute everything because we have limited computational resources. No,

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: I think it's not a bias of the humans, but it's objectively simple. I mean, of course,

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: you never know. Maybe there's some corners very far out in the universe or super, super tiny below

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: the nucleus of atoms or parallel universes which are not nice and simple, but there's no evidence

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: for that, and we should apply Occam's razor and choose the simplest tree consistent with it,

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: but also it's a little bit self-referential. So maybe a quick pause. What is Occam's razor?

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: So Occam's razor says that you should not multiply entities beyond necessity, which if you translate

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: it into proper English, and in the scientific context means that if you have two theories or

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: hypotheses or models which equally well describe the phenomenon, your study or the data, you should

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: choose the more simple one. So that's just the principle? Yes. That's not like a provable

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: law perhaps? Perhaps. We'll kind of discuss it and think about it, but what's the intuition of why

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: the simpler answer is the one that is likelier to be more correct descriptor of whatever we're

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: talking about? I believe that Occam's razor is probably the most important principle in science.

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: I mean, of course we lead logical deduction and we do experimental design, but science is about

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: understanding the world, finding models of the world, and we can come up with crazy complex

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: models which explain everything but predict nothing, but the simple model seem to have

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: predictive power and it's a valid question why. And there are two answers to that. You can just

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: accept it. That is the principle of science and we use this principle and it seems to be successful.

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: We don't know why, but it just happens to be. Or you can try, you know, find another principle

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: which explains Occam's razor. And if we start with the assumption that the world is governed

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: by simple rules, then there's a bias towards simplicity and applying Occam's razor

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: is the mechanism to finding these rules. And actually in a more quantitative sense,

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: and we come back to that later in case of somnolent deduction, you can rigorously prove that.

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: You have to assume that the world is simple, then Occam's razor is the best you can do in a certain

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: sense. So I apologize for the romanticized question, but why do you think outside of its

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: effectiveness, why do you think we find simplicity so appealing as human beings? Why does E equals

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: MC squared seem so beautiful to us humans? I guess mostly in general, many things can be explained

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: by an evolutionary argument. And you know, there's some artifacts in humans which, you know,

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: are just artifacts and not necessarily necessary. But with this beauty and simplicity, it's,

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: I believe, at least the core is about, like science, finding regularities in the world,

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: understanding the world, which is necessary for survival, right? You know, if I look

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: at a bush, right, and I just see noise, and there is a tiger, right, and eats me, then I'm dead.

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: But if I try to find a pattern, and we know that humans are prone to find more patterns in data

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: than they are, you know, like the Mars face and all these things, but this bias towards finding

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: patterns, even if they are non- but I mean, it's best, of course, if they are, yeah, helps us for survival.

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: Yeah, that's fascinating. I haven't thought really about the... I thought I just loved science,

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: but indeed, in terms of just for survival purposes, there is an evolutionary argument for why

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: we find the work of Einstein so beautiful. Maybe a quick small tangent, could you describe what

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: Solomonov induction is? Yeah, so that's a theory which I claim, and Mr. Solomonov sort of claimed

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: a long time ago that this solves the big philosophical problem of induction, and I

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: believe the claim is essentially true, and what it does is the following. So, okay, for the picky

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: listener, induction can be interpreted narrowly and widely. Narrow means inferring models from data,

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: and widely means also then using these models for doing predictions, so prediction is also part of

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: the induction. So I'm a little sloppy sort of with the terminology, and maybe that comes from

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: Ray Solomonov being sloppy. Maybe I shouldn't say that. He can't complain anymore. So let me explain

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: a little bit this theory in simple terms. So assume we have a data sequence, make it very simple,

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: the simplest one, say 11111, and you see 100 ones. What do you think comes next? The natural answer,

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: I must speed up a little bit. The natural answer is, of course, one. And the question is why?

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: Well, we see a pattern there. There's a one, and we repeat it. And why should it suddenly after

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: 100 ones be different? So what we're looking for is simple explanations or models for the data we

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: have. And now the question is, a model has to be presented in a certain language. In which language

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: do we use? In science, we want formal languages, and we can use mathematics, or we can use programs

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: on a computer, so abstractly on a Turing machine, for instance, or it can be a general purpose

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: computer. And there are, of course, lots of models. You can say maybe it's 100 ones, and then 100

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: zeros, and 100 ones. That's a model, right? But they are simpler models. There's a model print one

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: loop. That also explains the data. And if you push it to the extreme, you are looking for the

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: shortest program, which, if you run this program, reproduces the data you have. It will not stop. It

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: will continue, naturally. And this you take for your prediction. And on the sequence of ones,

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: it's very plausible, right? That print one loop is the shortest program. We can give some more

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: complex examples, like one, two, three, four, five. What comes next? The short program is again,

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: you know, counter. And so that is, roughly speaking, how solenoid induction works.

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: The extra twist is that it can also deal with noisy data. So if you have, for instance, a coin

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: flip, say a biased coin, which comes up head with 60% probability, then it will predict. It will

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: learn and figure this out. And after a while, it predicts, oh, the next coin flip will be head

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: with probability 60%. So it's the stochastic version of that.

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: But the goal is, the dream is always the search for the short program.

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: Yes. Yeah. Well, in solomonic induction, precisely what you do is, so you have a

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: combination of the two. So what you do is, so you combine, so looking for the shortest program

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: is like applying Opax-Razor, like looking for the simplest theory. There's also Epicorus principle,

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: which says, if you have multiple hypotheses, which equally well describe your data, don't

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: discard any of them. Keep all of them around. You never know. And you can put that together

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: and say, okay, I have a bias towards simplicity, but it don't rule out the larger models.

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: What we do is, we weigh the shorter models higher and the longer models lower. And you

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: use a Bayesian techniques. You have a prior, which is precisely two to the minus the complexity of

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: the program. And you weigh all this hypothesis and take this mixture. And then you get also

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: this stochasticity in. Yeah. Like many of your ideas, that's just

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: a beautiful idea of weighing based on the simplicity of the program. I love that. That

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: seems to me, maybe a very human-centric concept, seems to be a very appealing way

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: of discovering good programs in this world. You've used the term compression quite a bit.

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: I think it's a beautiful idea. We just talked about simplicity and maybe science or just

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: all of our intellectual pursuits is basically the attempt to compress the complexity all

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: around us into something simple. So what does this word mean to you, compression?

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: I essentially have already explained it. So compression means for me, finding short programs

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: for the data or the phenomenon at hand. You could interpret it more widely as finding

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: simple theories, which can be mathematical theories or maybe even informal, like just

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: in words. Compression means finding short descriptions, explanations, programs for the

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: data. Do you see science as a kind of our human

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: attempt at compression? So we're speaking more generally because when you say programs,

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: you're kind of zooming in on a particular sort of almost like a computer science,

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: artificial intelligence focus. But do you see all of human endeavor as a kind of compression?

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: Well, at least all of science I see as an endeavor of compression, not all of humanity maybe.

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: Well, there are also some other aspects of science like experimental design. We

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: create experiments specifically to get extra knowledge. That is then part of the decision

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: making process. But once we have the data to understand the data is essentially compression.

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: So I don't see any difference between compression, understanding and prediction.

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: So we're jumping around topics a little bit, but returning back to simplicity,

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: a fascinating concept of Kolmogorov complexity. So in your sense, do most objects in our

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: mathematical universe have high Kolmogorov complexity? And maybe what is, first of all,

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: what is Kolmogorov complexity? Okay, Kolmogorov complexity is a notion of simplicity or complexity.

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: And it takes the compression view to the extreme. So I explained before that if you have some data

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: sequence, just think about a file in a computer and best sort of just a string of bits. And

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: if you... And we have data compressors, like we compress big files into zip files with certain

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: compressors. And you can also produce self-extracting RKFs. That means as an executable,

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: if you run it, it reproduces your original file without needing an extra decompressor.

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: It's just a decompressor plus the RKF together in one. And now there are better and worse

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: compressors. And you can ask, what is the ultimate compressor? So what is the shortest possible

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: self-extracting RKF you could produce for a certain data set, which reproduces the data set? And the

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: length of this is called the Kolmogorov complexity. And arguably, that is the information content

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: in the data set. I mean, if the data set is very redundant or very boring, you can compress it very

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: well. So the information content should be low. And it is low according to this definition.

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: So it's the length of the shortest program that summarizes the data?

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: Yes. Yeah.

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: And what's your sense of our sort of universe when we think about the different...

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: The different objects in our universe that we try, concepts or whatever, at every level,

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: do they have higher or low Kolmogorov complexity? So what's the hope? Do we have a lot of hope in

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: being able to summarize much of our world? That's a tricky and difficult question. So

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: as I said before, I believe that the whole universe based on the evidence we have

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: is very simple. So it has a very short description. Sorry, to linger on that, the whole universe,

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: what does that mean? Do you mean at the very basic fundamental level in order to create the

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: universe? Yes. Yeah. So you need a very short program and you run it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: To get the thing going.

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: To get the thing going and then it will reproduce our universe. There's a problem with noise.

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: We can come back to that later, possibly.

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: Is noise a problem or is it a problem?

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: Is noise a problem or is it a bugger feature?

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: I would say it makes our life as a scientist really, really much harder. I mean, think about

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: without noise, we wouldn't need all of the statistics. But then maybe we wouldn't feel

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: like there's a free will. Maybe we need that for the...

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: This is an illusion that noise can give you free will.

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: At least in that way, it's a feature. But also if you don't have noise, you have chaotic phenomena,

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: which are effectively like noise. So we can't get away with statistics even then. I mean,

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: think about rolling a dice and forget about quantum mechanics and you know exactly how you

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: you throw it. But I mean, it's still so hard to compute the trajectory that effectively

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: it is best to model it as coming out with a number, with probability one over six.

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: But from this set of philosophical, Kolmogorov complexity perspective, if we didn't have noise,

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: then arguably you could describe the whole universe as standard model plus generativity.

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: I mean, we don't have a theory of everything yet, but sort of assuming we are close to it or have

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: it here, plus the initial conditions, which may hopefully be simple. And then you just run it and

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: then you would reproduce the universe. But that's all by noise or by chaotic systems or by initial

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: conditions, which may be complex. So now if we don't take the whole universe with just a subset,

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: just take planet Earth. Planet Earth cannot be compressed into a couple of equations.

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: This is a hugely complex system. So interesting. So when you look at the window,

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: like the whole thing might be simple, but when you just take a small window, then-

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: It may become complex and that may be counterintuitive, but there's a very nice analogy.

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: The library of all books. So imagine you have a normal library with interesting books and you go

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: there. Great. Lots of information and quite complex. So now I create a library which contains

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: all possible books, say of 500 pages. So the first book just has AAAA over all the pages.

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: The next book AAAA and ends with B and so on. I create this library of all books. I can write

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: a super short program which creates this library. So this library, which has all books, has zero

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: information content. And you take a subset of this library and suddenly you have a lot of

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: information in there. So that's fascinating. I think one of the most beautiful mathematical objects

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: that at least today seems to be understudied or under talked about is cellular automata.

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: What lessons do you draw from sort of the game of life for cellular automata where you start with

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: the simple rules, just like you're describing with the universe and somehow complexity emerges? Do

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: you feel like you have an intuitive grasp on the fascinating behavior of such systems where

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: like you said, some chaotic behavior could happen, some complexity could emerge,

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: it could die out in some very rigid structures? Do you have a sense about cellular automata that

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: somehow transfers maybe to the bigger questions of our universe? Yeah, the cellular automata and

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: especially the Conway's game of life is really great because the rules are so simple. You can

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: explain it to every child and even by hand you can simulate a little bit. And you see these

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: beautiful patterns emerge and people have proven that it's even Turing complete. You cannot just

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: use a computer to simulate game of life, but you can also use game of life to simulate any computer.

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: That is truly amazing. And it's the prime example probably to

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: demonstrate that very simple rules can lead to very rich phenomena. And people sometimes,

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: you know, how is chemistry and biology so rich? I mean, this can't be based on simple rules.

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: But no, we know quantum electrodynamics describes all of chemistry. And we come later back to that.

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: I claim intelligence can be described in one single equation, this very rich phenomenon.

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: You asked also about whether I understand this phenomenon. It's probably not.

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: And there's this saying, you never understand really things, you just get used to them.

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: And I think I'm pretty used to cellular automata. So you believe that you understand now why this

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: phenomenon happens. But I give you a different example. I didn't play too much with Conway's

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: Game of Life, but a little bit more with fractals and with the Mandelbrot set and

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: these beautiful patterns. Just look, Mandelbrot set. And well, when the computers were really

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: slow and I just had a black and white monitor and programmed my own programs in assembler too.

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: Assembler, wow. Wow. You're legit.

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: To get these fractals on the screen. And it was mesmerized. And much later. So I returned to this,

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: every couple of years. And then I tried to understand what is going on. And you can understand

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: a little bit. So I tried to derive the locations. There are these circles and the apple shape.

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: And then you have smaller Mandelbrot sets recursively in this set. And there's a way to

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: mathematically by solving high order polynomials to figure out where these centers are and what

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: size they are approximately. And by sort of mathematically approaching this problem,

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: you slowly get a feeling of why things are like they are. And that sort of isn't, you know,

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: first step to understanding why this rich phenomenon.

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: Do you think it's possible? What's your intuition? Do you think it's possible to reverse engineer

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: and find the short program that generated these fractals?

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: Sort of by looking at the fractals? Well, in principle, yes. So, I mean, in principle,

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: what you can do is you take any data set. You take these fractals or you take whatever your data set,

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: whatever you have. Say a picture of Conway's Game of Life. And you run through all programs.

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: You take a program size one, two, three, four, and all these programs around them,

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: all in parallel in so-called dovetailing fashion. Give them computational resources,

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: first one 50%, second one half resources, and so on. And let them run. Wait until they

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: hold, give an output, compare it to your data. And if some of these programs produce the correct data,

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: then you stop and then you have already some program. It may be a long program because it's

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: faster. And then you continue and you get shorter and shorter programs until you eventually find

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: the shortest program. The interesting thing, you can never know whether it's the shortest program

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: because there could be an even shorter program, which is just even slower.

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: And you just have to wait here. But asymptotically, and actually after finite time,

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: you have the shortest program. So, this is a theoretical but completely impractical way

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: of finding the underlying structure in every data set. And that is what Solomov induction does and

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: Kolmogorov complexity. In practice, of course, we have to approach the problem more intelligently.

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: And then if you take resource limitations into account, there's for instance, the field of

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: pseudo random numbers. And these are random numbers. So, these are deterministic sequences,

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: but no algorithm, which is fast, fast means runs in polynomial time, can detect that it's

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: actually deterministic. So, we can produce interesting, I mean, random numbers, maybe not

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: that interesting, but just an example. We can produce complex looking data and we can then

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: prove that no fast algorithm can detect the underlying pattern. Which is unfortunately,

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: that's a big challenge for our search for simple programs in the space of artificial intelligence,

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: perhaps. Yes, it definitely is for artificial intelligence. And it's quite surprising that it's,

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: I can't say easy. I mean, physicists worked really hard to find these theories, but apparently it was

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: possible for human minds to find these simple rules in the universe. It could have been

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: different, right? It could have been different. It's awe-inspiring. So, let me ask another absurdly

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: measures an agent's ability to perform well in a wide range of environments.

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: So, that doesn't sound very impressive, but these words have been very carefully chosen.

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: And there is a mathematical theory behind that, and we come back to that later. And if you look

body.input: at this definition by itself, it seems like, yeah, okay, but it seems a lot of things are missing.

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: But if you think it through, then you realize that most, and I claim all of the other traits,

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: at least of rational intelligence, which we usually associate with intelligence,

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: are emergent phenomena from this definition, like creativity, memorization, planning, knowledge.

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: You all need that in order to perform well in a wide range of environments.

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: So, you don't have to explicitly mention that in a definition.

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: Interesting. So, yeah, so the consciousness, abstract reasoning, all these kinds of things

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: are just emergent phenomena that help you in towards, can you say the definition again?

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: So, multiple environments. Did you mention the word goals?

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: we want to specify there should be a goal.

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: Yeah, but perform well is sort of what does it mean? It's the same problem.

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: Yeah. There's a little bit of gray area, but it's much closer to something that could be formalized.

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75
