body.input: important, but at this stage, we can just think about predicting, say, stock market data, whether

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: data or IQ sequences, one, two, three, four, five, what comes next. So of course, our actions

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: affect what we're doing, but I'll come back to that in a second.

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: So, and I'll keep just interrupting. So just to draw a line between prediction and planning,

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: what do you mean by prediction in this way? It's trying to predict the environment without your

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: long-term action in that environment. What is prediction?

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: Okay. If you want to put the actions in now, okay, then let's put in now.

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: We don't have to put them now. Scratch it, dumb question. Okay.

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: So the simplest form of prediction is that you just have data which you passively observe,

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: observe, and you want to predict what happens without interfering. As I said, weather forecasting,

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: stock market, IQ sequences, or just anything. Okay. And Solomons theory of induction based

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: on compression. So you look for the shortest program, which describes your data sequence,

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: and then you take this program, run it, which reproduces your data sequence by definition,

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: and then you let it continue running, and then it will produce some predictions. And you can

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: rigorously prove that for any prediction task, this is essentially the best possible predictor.

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: Of course, if there's a prediction task or a task which is unpredictable, like fair coin flips,

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: yeah, I cannot predict the next fair coin flip. What Solomonov does is says, okay, next

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: head is probably 50%. It's the best you can do. So if something is unpredictable, Solomonov will

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: also not magically predict it. But if there is some pattern and predictability, then Solomonov

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: induction will figure that out eventually, and not just eventually, but rather quickly,

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: and you can have proof convergence rates, whatever your data is. So that is pure magic in a sense.

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: What's the catch? Well, the catch is that it's not computable, and we come back to that later.

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: You cannot just implement it even with Google resources here and run it and predict the stock

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: market and become rich. I mean, Ray Solomonov already tried it at the time.

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: But the basic task is you're in the environment, and you're interacting with the environment to

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: try to learn a model of that environment, and the model is in the space of all these programs,

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: and your goal is to get a bunch of programs that are simple.

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: And so let's go to the actions now. But actually, good that you asked. Usually I skip this part,

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: although there is also a minor contribution, which I did, so the action part, but I usually

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: sort of just jump to the decision part. So let me explain the action part now. Thanks for asking.

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: Yes. So you have to modify it a little bit by now not just predicting a sequence which just

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: comes to you, but you have an observation, then you act somehow, and then you want to predict

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: the next observation based on the past observation and your action. Then you take the next action.

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: You don't care about predicting it because you're doing it. And then you get the next observation,

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: and you want, well, before you get it, you want to predict it again based on your past

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: action and observation sequence. You just condition extra on your actions.

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: There's an interesting alternative that you also try to predict your own actions.

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: If you want... In the past or the future?

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: In your future actions. That's interesting.

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: Wait, let me wrap. I think my brain is broke.

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: We should maybe discuss that later after I've explained the IC model. That's an interesting

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: variation. But that is a really interesting variation. And a quick comment, I don't know if

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: you want to insert that in here, but you're looking at that in terms of observations,

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: you're looking at the entire big history, the long history of the observations.

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: Exactly. That's very important, the whole history from birth of the agent. And we can come back to

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: that also why this is important. Often in RL, you have MDPs, micro decision processes,

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: which are much more limiting. Okay. So now we can predict conditioned on actions. So even if we

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: influence environment, but prediction is not all we want to do. We also want to act really in the

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: world. And the question is how to choose the actions. And we don't want to greedily choose

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: the actions. Just what is best in the next time step. And first I should say, how do we measure

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: performance? So we measure performance by giving the agent reward. That's the so-called reinforcement

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: learning framework. So every time step, you can give it a positive reward or negative reward,

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: or maybe no reward. It could be a very scarce, right? Like if you play chess, just at the end

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: of the game, you give plus one for winning or minus one for losing. So in the IxC framework,

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: that's completely sufficient. So occasionally you give a reward signal and you ask the agent

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: to maximize reward, but not greedily sort of the next one, next one, because that's very bad in the

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: long run if you're greedy. But over the lifetime of the agent. So let's assume the agent lives for M

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: time steps, as they dies in sort of a hundred years sharp. That's just the simplest model to explain.

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: So it looks at the future reward sum and ask what is my action sequence, or actually more precisely

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: my policy, which leads in expectation, because I don't know the world, to the maximum reward sum.

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: Let me give you an analogy. In chess, for instance, we know how to play optimally in theory.

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: It's just a mini max strategy. I play the move, which seems best to me under the assumption that

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: the opponent plays the move, which is best for him. So best, so worst for me under the assumption that

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: I play again, the best move. And then you have this expecting max tree to the end of the game.

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: And then you back propagate and then you get the best possible move. So that is the optimal

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: strategy, which for Neumann already figured out a long time ago for playing adversarial games.

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: Luckily, or maybe unluckily for the theory, it becomes harder. The world is not always adversarial.

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: So it can be if the other humans even cooperative, or nature is usually, I mean, the dead nature is

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: stochastic. Things just happen randomly or don't care about you. So what you have to take into

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: account is the noise and not necessarily adversariality. So you replace the minimum on

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: the opponent's side by an expectation, which is general enough to include also adversarial cases.

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: So now instead of a mini max strategy, you have an expected max strategy. So far so good. So that

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: is well known. It's called sequential decision theory. But the question is on which probability

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: distribution do you base that? If I have the true probability distribution, like say I play

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: Begumman, right? There's dice and there's certain randomness involved. Yeah, I can calculate

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: probabilities and feed it in the expect the max or the sequential decision tree, come up with the

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: optimal decision if I have enough compute. But for the real world, we don't know that. What is the

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: probability the driver in front of me breaks? I don't know. So it depends on all kinds of things

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: and especially new situations, I don't know. So this is this unknown thing about prediction.

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: And there's where Solomanov comes in. So what you do is in sequential decision theory, you just

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: replace the true distribution, which we don't know, by this universal distribution. I didn't

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: explicitly talk about it, but this is used for universal prediction and plug it into the

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: sequential decision mechanism. And then you get the best of both worlds. You have a long term

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: planning agent, but it doesn't need to know anything about the world because the Solomanov

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: induction part learns. Can you explicitly try to describe the universal distribution?

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: And how Solomanov induction plays a role here? I'm trying to understand.

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: So what it does it, so in the simplest case, I said, take the shortest program describing your

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: data, run it, have a prediction which would be deterministic. But you should not just take the

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: shortest program, but also consider the longer ones, but keep it lower a priori probability.

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: So in the Bayesian framework, you say a priori any distribution, you have a probability that

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: is a model or a stochastic program, has a certain a priori probability, which is two to the minus,

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: and why two to the minus length? I could explain length of this program. So longer programs are

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: punished a priori. And then you multiply it with the so-called likelihood function, which is,

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: as the name suggests, is how likely is this model given the data at hand. So if you have a very

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: wrong model, it's very unlikely that this model is true, and so it is very small number. So even

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: if the model is simple, it gets penalized by that. And what you do is then you take just the sum,

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: this is the average over it. And this gives you a probability distribution, so-called

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: universal distribution of Solomanov distribution. So it's weighed by the simplicity of the program

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: and likelihood. Yes. It's kind of a nice idea. Yeah. So, okay. And then you said there's you're

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: playing N or M, or forgot the letter, steps into the future. So how difficult is that problem?

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: What's involved there? Okay. So basic optimization problem? What are we talking about? Yeah. So you

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: have a planning problem up to horizon M, and that's exponential time in the horizon M, which is,

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: I mean, it's computable, but intractable. I mean, even for chess, it's already intractable

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: to do that exactly and for goal. But it could be also discounted kind of framework where-

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: Yeah. So having a hard horizon at a hundred years is just for simplicity of discussing the model.

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: And also sometimes the math is simple. But there are lots of variations. It's actually a quite

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: interesting parameter. There's nothing really problematic about it, but it's very interesting.

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: So for instance, you think, no, let's let the parameter M tend to infinity, right? You want an

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: agent which lives forever, right? If you do it naively, you have two problems. First, the mathematics

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: breaks down because you have an infinite reward sum, which may give infinity and getting reward

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: 0.1 in the time step is infinity and giving a reward one every time step is infinity. So equally good.

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: Not really what we want. Other problem is that if you have an infinite life, you can be lazy for as

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: long as you want for 10 years and then catch up with the same expected reward. And think about

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: yourself or maybe some friends or so. If they knew they lived forever, why work hard now?

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: Just enjoy your life and then catch up later. So that's another problem with infinite horizon.

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: And you mentioned, yes, we can go to discounting, but then the standard discounting is so-called

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: geometric discounting. So a dollar today is about worth as much as $1.05 tomorrow. So if you do the

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: so-called geometric discounting, you have introduced an effective horizon. So the agent is now motivated

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: to look ahead a certain amount of time effectively. It's like a moving horizon. And for any fixed

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: effective horizon, there is a problem to solve, which requires larger horizons. So if I look ahead,

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: five time steps, I'm a terrible chess player. I need to look ahead longer. If I play Go,

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: I probably have to look ahead even longer. So for every horizon, there is a problem which this horizon

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: cannot solve. But I introduced the so-called near harmonic horizon, which goes down with one over

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: T rather than exponentially T, which produces an agent which effectively looks into the future

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: proportional to each age. So if it's five years old, it plans for five years. If it's 100 years old,

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: it then plans for 100 years. And it's a little bit similar to humans too, right? I mean, children

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: don't plan ahead very long, but then we get adult, we play ahead more longer. Maybe when we get very

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: old, I mean, we know that we don't live forever, maybe then our horizon shrinks again.

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: So that's really interesting. So adjusting the horizon, is there some mathematical benefit of

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: that or is it just a nice... I mean, intuitively, empirically, it would probably be a good idea to

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: push the horizon back, extend the horizon as you experience more of the world. But is there some

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: mathematical conclusions here that are beneficial? With solomonic reductions or prediction part,

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: we have extremely strong finite time, finite data results. So you have so and so much data,

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: then you lose so and so much. So the theory is really great. With the ICSI model with the

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: planning part, many results are only asymptotic, which well, this is- What does asymptotic mean?

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: Asymptotic means you can prove for instance, that in the long run, if the agent acts long enough,

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: then it performs optimal or some nice thing happens. But you don't know how fast it converges.

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: So it may converge fast, but we're just not able to prove it because of difficult problem.

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: Or maybe there's a bug in the model so that it's really that slow. So that is what asymptotic means

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: eventually, but we don't know how fast. And if I give the agent a fixed horizon M, then I cannot

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: prove asymptotic results. So I mean, if it dies in 100 years, then in 100 years it's over. I cannot

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: say eventually. So this is the advantage of the discounting that I can prove asymptotic results.

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: So just to clarify, so I, okay, I've built up a model. Well, now in the moment, I have this

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: way of looking several steps ahead. How do I pick what action I will take?

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: It's like with a playing chess, right? You do this minimax. In this case here, do you expect the

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: max based on the Solomons of distribution? You propagate back and then while an action falls out,

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: the action which maximizes the future expected reward on the Solomons of distribution. And then

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: you just take this action and then repeat it. Then you get a new observation and you've

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: beat it in this action observation. Then you repeat and the reward. So on. Yeah. So you're

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: able to, yeah. And then maybe you can even predict your own action. I love that idea. But okay, this

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: big framework, what is it? I mean, it's kind of a beautiful mathematical framework to think about

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: artificial general intelligence. What can you, what does it help you into it about how to build such

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: systems or maybe from another perspective, what does it help us in understanding AGI?

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: So when I started in the field, I was always interested in two things. One was AGI. The name

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: didn't exist then. What's called general AI or strong AI. And the physics theory of everything.

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: So I switched back and forth between computer science and physics quite often.

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: You said the theory of everything. The theory of everything.

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: It was basically the biggest problems before all of humanity.

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: proven that this is the most intelligent agents, which anybody could build in quotation mark,

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: because it's just mathematical and you need infinite compute. But this is the limit.

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: And this is completely specified. It's not just a framework and, you know,

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: tree, blah, blah, blah, and so on. So we can do that also with the ICSI model, but for general AI.

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: It can also inspire those and most of most researchers go bottom up, right? They have

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: their systems that try to make it more general, more intelligent. It can inspire in which direction

body.input: to go. What do you mean by that? So if you have some choice to make, right? So how should I evaluate

body.input: point of view, but you can look at it and see, ah, yeah, maybe, you know, I can take some aspects

body.input: and, you know, instead of Kolmogorov complexity, that just takes some compressors, which has been

body.input: developed so far. And for the planning, well, we have UCT, which has also, you know, been used in

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: Go. And at least it's inspired me a lot to have this formal definition. And if you look at other

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: fields, you know, like I always come back to physics because I have a physics background,

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: think about the phenomenon of energy. That was long time a mysterious concept. And at some point,

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: it was completely formalized. And that really helped a lot. And you can point out a lot of these

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: things, which were first mysterious and vague, and then they have been rigorously formalized.

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: Speed and acceleration has been confused, right, until it was formally defined. Yeah,

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: there was a time like this. And people, you know, often, you know, who don't have any background,

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: you know, still confuse it. So, and this ICSI model or the intelligence definitions,

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: which is sort of the dual to it, we come back to that later, formalizes the notion of intelligence

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: uniquely and rigorously. So in a sense, it serves as kind of the light at the end of the tunnel.

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: Yes, yeah. So, I mean, there's a million questions I could ask her. So maybe,

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: kind of, okay, let's feel around in the dark a little bit. So there's been here a deep mind,

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: but in general, been a lot of breakthrough ideas, just like we've been saying around

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: reinforcement learning. So how do you see the progress in reinforcement learning is different?

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: Like, which subset of ICSI does it occupy? The current, like you said, maybe the Markov

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: assumption is made quite often in reinforcement learning. There's other assumptions made in order

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: to make the system work. What do you see as the difference connection between reinforcement

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: learning and ICSI? So the major difference is that essentially all other approaches,

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: they make stronger assumptions. So in reinforcement learning, the Markov assumption

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: is that the next state or next observation only depends on the previous observation and not the

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: whole history, which makes, of course, the mathematics much easier rather than dealing

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: with histories. Of course, they profit from it also because then you have algorithms that run on

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: current computers and do something practically useful. But for general AI, all the assumptions

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: which are made by other approaches, we know already now they are limiting. So for instance,

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: usually you need an agodicity assumption in the MDP frameworks in order to learn.

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: Agodicity essentially means that you can recover from your mistakes and that there are no traps in

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: the environment. And if you make this assumption, then essentially you can go back to a previous

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: state, go there a couple of times and then learn what statistics and what the state is like, and

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: then in the long run perform well in this state. But there are no fundamental problems. But in real

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: life, we know there can be one single action. One second of being inattentive while driving a car

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: fast can ruin the rest of my life. I can become quadriplegic or whatever. And there's no recovery

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: anymore. So the real world is not ergodic, I always say. There are traps and there are situations

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: we are not recovered from. And very little theory has been developed for this case.

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: What do you see in the context of AIXE as the role of exploration?

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: You mentioned in the real world, we can get into trouble when we make the wrong decisions and really

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: pay for it. But exploration seems to be fundamentally important for learning about this world, for

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: gaining new knowledge. So is exploration baked in? Another way to ask it, what are the parameters

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: of AIXE that can be controlled? Yeah, I say the good thing is that there are no parameters to

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: control. Some other people track knobs to control and you can do that. I mean, you can modify AIXE

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: so that you have some knobs to play with if you want to. But the exploration is directly baked in

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: and that comes from the Bayesian learning and the long-term planning. So these together

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: already imply exploration. You can nicely and explicitly prove that for simple problems like

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: so-called bandit problems where you say to give a real-world example, say you have two medical

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: treatments, A and B, you don't know the effectiveness, you try A a little bit, B a little bit, but

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: you don't want to harm too many patients. So you have to sort of trade off exploring. And at some

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: point you want to explore and you can do the mathematics and figure out the optimal strategy.

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: The Bayesian agents are also non-Bayesian agents, but it shows that this Bayesian framework by taking

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: a prior over possible worlds, doing the Bayesian mixture, then the base optimal decision with

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: long-term planning that is important automatically implies exploration also to the proper extent,

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: not too much exploration and not too little in these very simple settings. In the AIXE model,

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: I was also able to prove that it is a self-optimizing strategy.

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: More asymptotic optimality theorems, although they're only asymptotic, not finite time bounds.

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: So it seems like the long-term planning is really important, but the long-term part of

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: the planning is really important. And also, maybe a quick tangent, how important do you think is

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: removing the Markov assumption and looking at the full history? Sort of intuitively, of course,

body.input: it's important, but is it fundamentally transformative to the entirety of the problem?

body.input: What's your sense of it? Because we make that assumption quite often,

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: just throwing away the past.

body.input: because that are rewards. It seems to be an important part. The rewards are kind of given

body.input: to the system. For a lot of people, the specification of the objective function

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: is a key part of intelligence. The agent itself figuring out what is important.

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: What do you think about that? Is it possible within the IAC framework to yourself discover

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: the reward based on which you should operate? Okay. That will be a long answer.

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: So, and it is a very interesting question. And I'm asked a lot about this question. Where do

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: the rewards come from? And that depends. Yeah. So, and I give you now a couple of answers. So

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: if we want to build agents, now let's start simple. So let's assume we want to build an agent,

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: based on the IAC model, which performs a particular task. Let's start with something super simple,

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: like, I mean, super simple, like playing chess or go or something. Yeah. Then you just, you know,

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: the reward is, you know, winning the game is plus one, losing the game is minus one. Done. You apply

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: this agent. If you have enough compute, you let itself play and it will learn the rules of the

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: game. We'll play perfect chess after some while. Problem solved. Okay. So if you have more complicated

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: problems, then you may believe that you have the right reward, but it's not. So a nice cute example

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: is elevator control. That is also in Rich Sutton's book, which is a great book, by the way.

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: So you control the elevator and you think, well, maybe the reward should be coupled to how long

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: people wait in front of the elevator. You know, long wait is bad. You program it and you do it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: And what happens is the elevator eagerly picks up all the people, but never drops them off.

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: So then you realize, maybe the time in the elevator also counts. So you minimize the sum.

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: Yeah. And the elevator does that, but never picks up the people in the 10th floor,

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: in the top floor, because in expectation, it's not worth it. Just let them stay.

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: So even in apparently simple problems, you can make mistakes. Yeah. And that's

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: what in more serious contexts, AGI safety researchers consider. So now let's go back to

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: general agents. So assume we want to build an agent, which is generally useful to humans.

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: Yes, we have a household robot here and it should do all kinds of tasks. So in this case,

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: the human should give the reward on the fly. I mean, maybe it's pre-trained in the factory

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: and that there's some sort of internal reward for the battery level or whatever. But

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: so it does the dishes badly. You punish the robot, it does it good, you reward the robot,

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: and then train it to do a new task. Like a child, right? So you need the human in the loop if you

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: want a system which is useful to the human. And as long as this agent stays sub-human level,

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: that should work reasonably well, apart from these examples. It becomes critical if they become

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: on a human level. It's the same with children, small children. You have reasonably well under

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: control, they become older. The reward technique doesn't work so well anymore. So then finally,

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: so these would be agents which are just, you could say, slaves to the humans. So if you are

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: more ambitious and just say we want to build a new species of intelligent beings, we put them on a

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: new planet and we want them to develop this planet or whatever. So we don't give them any reward.

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: So what could we do? And you could try to come up with some reward functions like it should

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: maintain itself, the robot, it should maybe multiply, build more robots, right? And maybe

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: all kinds of things which you find useful. But that's pretty hard, right? What does self-maintenance

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: mean? What does it mean to build a copy? Should it be exact copy, an approximate copy? And so that's

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: really hard. But Laurent Assort, also at DeepMind, developed a beautiful model. So it just took the

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: ICSI model and coupled the rewards to information gain. So he said the reward is proportional to

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: how much the agent had learned about the world. And you can rigorously formally uniquely define

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: that in terms of other versions, okay? So if you put that in, you get a copy of the robot,

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: so if you put that in, you get a completely autonomous agent. And actually, interestingly,

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: for this agent, we can prove much stronger result than for the general agent, which is also nice.

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: And if you let this agent lose, it will be, in a sense, the optimal scientist. It is absolutely

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: curious to learn as much as possible about the world. And of course, it will also have a lot of

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: instrumental goals, right? In order to learn, it needs to at least survive, right? That agent is

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: not good for anything. So it needs to have self-preservation. And if it builds small helpers

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: acquiring more information, it will do that. If exploration, space exploration or whatever,

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: is necessary, right? To gathering information and develop it. So it has a lot of instrumental goals

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: following on this information gain. And this agent is completely autonomous of us.

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: No rewards necessary anymore. Yeah. Of course, it could find a way to game the concept of

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: information and get stuck in that library that you mentioned beforehand with a very large number

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: of books. The first agent had this problem. It would get stuck in front of an old TV screen,

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: which has just had white noise. Yeah, white noise, yeah. But the second version can deal with at

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: least stochasticity. Well, yeah. What about curiosity? This kind of word, curiosity, creativity,

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: is that kind of the reward function being of getting new information? Is that similar to

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: idea of kind of injecting exploration for its own sake inside the reward function? Do you find this

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: at all appealing, interesting? I think that's a nice definition. Curiosity is reward, sorry,

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: curiosity is exploration for its own sake. Yeah, I would accept that. But most curiosity,

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: well, in humans and especially in children, yeah, is not just for its own sake, but for actually

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: learning about the environment and for behaving better. So I think most curiosity is tied in the

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: end towards performing better. Well, okay. So if intelligence systems need to have this reward

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: function, let me, you're an intelligence system currently passing the TORN test quite effectively.

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: What's the reward function of our human intelligence existence? What's the reward

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: function that Marcus Hodder is operating under? Okay, to the first question, the biological

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: reward function is to survive and to spread. And very few humans sort of are able to overcome

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: this biological reward function. But we live in a very nice world where we have lots of spare time

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: and can still survive and spread. So we can develop arbitrary other interests, which is quite

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: interesting. On top of that. On top of that, yeah. But the survival and spreading sort of is,

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: I would say the goal or the reward function of humans, the core one.

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: I like how you avoided answering the second question, which a good intelligence system would.

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: Your own meaning of life and the reward function.

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: My own meaning of life and reward function is to find an AGI to build it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: Beautifully put. Okay. Let's dissect Ixie even further. So one of the assumptions is kind of

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: infinity keeps creeping up everywhere. What are your thoughts on kind of bounded rationality?

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: And sort of the nature of our existence and intelligence systems is that we're operating

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: always under constraints, under limited time, limited resources. How do you think about that

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: within the Ixie framework, within trying to create an AGI system that operates under these

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: constraints? Yeah, that is one of the criticisms about Ixie, that it ignores computation and

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: completely. And some people believe that intelligence is inherently tied to what's

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: bounded resources. What do you think on this one point? Do you think the bounded resources

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: are fundamental to intelligence? I would say that an intelligence notion,

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: which ignores computational limits is extremely useful. A good intelligence notion, which includes

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: these resources would be even more useful, but we don't have that yet. And so look at other fields

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: outside of computer science. Computational aspects never play a fundamental role.

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: You develop biological models for cells, something in physics, these theories, I mean, become more

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: and more crazy and harder and harder to compute. Well, in the end, of course, we need to do

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: something with this model, but this more nuisance than a feature. And I'm sometimes wondering if

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: artificial intelligence would not sit in a computer science department, but in a philosophy department,

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: then this computational focus would be probably significantly less. I mean, think about the

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: induction problem is more in the philosophy department. There's virtually no paper who cares

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: about how long it takes to compute the answer. That is completely secondary. Of course, once we

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: have figured out the first problem, so intelligence without computational resources, then the next

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: and very good question is, could we improve it by including computational resources? But nobody was

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: able to do that so far in an even halfway satisfactory manner. I like that, that in the

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: long run, the right department to belong to is philosophy. That's actually quite a deep idea,

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: or even to at least to think about big picture philosophical questions, big picture questions,

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: even in the computer science department. But you've mentioned approximation,

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: there's a lot of infinity, a lot of huge resources needed. Are there approximations to ICSE that

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: within ICSE framework that are useful? Yeah, we have developed a couple of approximations.

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: What we do there is that the Solomov induction part, which was find the shortest program

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: describing your data, we just replace it by standard data compressors.

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: The better compressors get, the better this part will become. We focus on a particular

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: compressor called context-free weighting, which is pretty amazing, not so well known,

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: has beautiful theoretical properties, also works reasonably well in practice.

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: We use that for the approximation of the induction and the learning and the prediction part.

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: For the planning part, we essentially just took the ideas from a computer go from 2006.

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: It was Chhabar Sepespare, also now a DeepMind, who developed the so-called UCT algorithm,

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: upper confidence bound for trees algorithm on top of the Monte Carlo tree search.

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: So we approximate this planning part by sampling. It's successful on some small toy problems.

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: We don't want to lose the generality. That's the handicap. If you want to be general,

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: you have to give up something. But this single agent was able to play small games like Kuhn

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: Poker and Tic Tac Toe and even Pac-Man. It's the same architecture, no change. The agent

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: doesn't know the rules of the game, really nothing all by itself or by a player with these environments.

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: So Jürgen Schmidhuber proposed something called Gertl Machines, which is a self-improving program

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: that rewrites its own code. Sort of mathematically or philosophically, what's the relationship

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: in your eyes, if you're familiar with it, between AXE and the Gertl Machines?

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: Yeah, familiar with it. He developed it while I was in his lab.

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: So the Gertl Machine, to explain it briefly, you give it a task. It could be a simple task

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: as finding prime factors in numbers. You can formally write it down. There's a very slow

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: algorithm to do that. Just try all the factors. Or play chess. Optimally, you write the algorithm

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: to minimax to the end of the game. So you write down what the Gertl Machine should do.

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: Then it will take part of its resources to run this program and other part of the resources

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: to improve this program. And when it finds an approved version, which provably computes the

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: same answer. So that's the key part. It needs to prove by itself that this change of program

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: still satisfies the original specification. And if it does so, then it replaces the original program

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: by the improved program. And by definition, it does the same job, but just faster. And then

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: it proves over it and over it. And it's developed in a way that all parts of this Gertl Machine

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: can self-improve, but it stays provably consistent with the original specification.

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: So from this perspective, it has nothing to do with AXE. But if you buy the Gertl Machine,

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: it would run AXE. But that takes forever. But then if it finds a provable speed up of AXE,

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: it would replace it by this and this and this. And maybe eventually it comes up with a model,

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: which is still the AXE model. Just for the knowledgeable reader, AXE is incomputable

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: and that can prove that therefore there is no problem with the original Gertl Machine.

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: AXE is incomputable and that can prove that therefore there cannot be a computable exact

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: algorithm computer. There needs to be some approximations and this is not dealt with

metadata.title: Podcast: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75

body.input: the Gertl Machine. So you have to do something about it. But there's the AXE TL model,

body.input: which is finitely computable, which we could put in.

body.input: Which part of AXE is non-computable?
