metadata.title: Podcast: Zach Bitter: Ultramarathon Running | Lex Fridman Podcast #205

body.input: Let's just give this another mile or two and then we can reassess if we need to in order to kind of figure out if I'm doing the right things or not.

metadata.title: Podcast: Zach Bitter: Ultramarathon Running | Lex Fridman Podcast #205

body.input: And I think like in that situation, you definitely probably want to lean more towards the Sam Harris approach with that because there's really no reason to.

metadata.title: Podcast: Zach Bitter: Ultramarathon Running | Lex Fridman Podcast #205

body.input: It's almost like the same thing you see with like just training and even nutrition to a degree where like some folks, they just want to be like kind of like drilled.

metadata.title: Podcast: Zach Bitter: Ultramarathon Running | Lex Fridman Podcast #205

body.input: They want to be like yelled at and said like get going, get doing this and that helps and that motivates and that helps them stay accountable.

metadata.title: Podcast: Zach Bitter: Ultramarathon Running | Lex Fridman Podcast #205

body.input: Other people need some softer love with it where it's like, you know, this isn't necessarily your fault.

metadata.title: Podcast: Zach Bitter: Ultramarathon Running | Lex Fridman Podcast #205

body.input: You were put in this environment that kind of created an atmosphere of lethargy and maybe poor nutritional choices and things like that.

metadata.title: Podcast: Zach Bitter: Ultramarathon Running | Lex Fridman Podcast #205

body.input: And like so but it's correctable. So we need to we need to step away from that.

metadata.title: Podcast: Zach Bitter: Ultramarathon Running | Lex Fridman Podcast #205

body.input: And we need to kind of start heading in the direction that we know is going to bear fruit down the road. And that person may respond better to that.

metadata.title: Podcast: Zach Bitter: Ultramarathon Running | Lex Fridman Podcast #205

body.input: So I think both those guys have great value with their approaches.

metadata.title: Podcast: Zach Bitter: Ultramarathon Running | Lex Fridman Podcast #205

body.input: They're just probably polar ends of the spectrum. And I think most people are probably going to benefit like anything.

metadata.title: Podcast: Zach Bitter: Ultramarathon Running | Lex Fridman Podcast #205

body.input: Right. You get the polarizing ones and those are going to work great for the polarizing people.

metadata.title: Podcast: Zach Bitter: Ultramarathon Running | Lex Fridman Podcast #205

body.input: But then most people are going to fit somewhere in the middle.

metadata.title: Podcast: Zach Bitter: Ultramarathon Running | Lex Fridman Podcast #205

body.input: So they're probably going to be able to kind of pull from both of those if they're able to sit down and kind of like assess which one's going to work better in which situation.

metadata.title: Podcast: Zach Bitter: Ultramarathon Running | Lex Fridman Podcast #205

body.input: So the quitting thing you mentioned, like the final stage, which actually I get to much quicker than you seem to, which is like, why am I doing this?

metadata.title: Podcast: Zach Bitter: Ultramarathon Running | Lex Fridman Podcast #205

body.input: I get there with basically anything I do. It's like this is this is probably the stupidest thing I've ever done is the feeling I get often.

metadata.title: Podcast: Zach Bitter: Ultramarathon Running | Lex Fridman Podcast #205

body.input: And then immediately you have these excuses. They're like, there's all these other better things you should be doing.

metadata.title: Podcast: Zach Bitter: Ultramarathon Running | Lex Fridman Podcast #205

body.input: Or or the other alternative that, like you said, I'm not prepared enough for this moment.

metadata.title: Podcast: Zach Bitter: Ultramarathon Running | Lex Fridman Podcast #205

body.input: I'll be much more prepared in two weeks for the next event.

metadata.title: Podcast: Zach Bitter: Ultramarathon Running | Lex Fridman Podcast #205

body.input: So like why let's try this again. Let's start over. Let's start over in two weeks.

metadata.title: Podcast: Zach Bitter: Ultramarathon Running | Lex Fridman Podcast #205

body.input: How do you deal with that quit?

metadata.title: Podcast: Zach Bitter: Ultramarathon Running | Lex Fridman Podcast #205

body.input: Like, so maybe do you still go through that process and by way of advice for people that are more sort of amateurish like me, how to deal with that quitting voice?

metadata.title: Podcast: Zach Bitter: Ultramarathon Running | Lex Fridman Podcast #205

body.input: I think a lot of times when the quitting voice kind of comes in, it what it does is it kind of just it comes in with the added disadvantage, I guess, in this situation of being kind of a narrow scoped view where you're looking at.

metadata.title: Podcast: Zach Bitter: Ultramarathon Running | Lex Fridman Podcast #205

body.input: Like what it's doing to you in the moment or how you're feeling in the moment versus how are you feeling about the whole process?

metadata.title: Podcast: Zach Bitter: Ultramarathon Running | Lex Fridman Podcast #205

body.input: So one thing that I started doing in 2019 and I think I don't think it's necessarily I think I think I think this was a big reason why I had one of my best racing seasons in 2019 that I had to that date.

metadata.title: Podcast: Zach Bitter: Ultramarathon Running | Lex Fridman Podcast #205

body.input: It was part of it was I started, I think, putting a little more emphasis on the big picture versus putting emphasis on like this is one opportunity or one day of work.

metadata.title: Podcast: Zach Bitter: Ultramarathon Running | Lex Fridman Podcast #205

body.input: And this is one one emotional kind of flare up. But how does that actually relate to my general broader picture?

metadata.title: Podcast: Zach Bitter: Ultramarathon Running | Lex Fridman Podcast #205

body.input: So when I decide to do a race or an event or something like that, it's often four or six months out ahead of time, you're planning to like kind of do a series of workouts and a flow of things where you're going through the process of getting fit, getting ready, preparing for the specifics of the day and all that stuff.

metadata.title: Podcast: Zach Bitter: Ultramarathon Running | Lex Fridman Podcast #205

body.input: And then you get to the race itself or the event itself. And it's very easy to look at that and think that's an isolation.

metadata.title: Podcast: Zach Bitter: Ultramarathon Running | Lex Fridman Podcast #205

body.input: Like I'm going to run 12 hours a day or I'm going to run 100 miles today or whatever it ends up being. And it's a lot easier to quit when you think to yourself, I'm 40 miles into 100 mile race.

metadata.title: Podcast: Zach Bitter: Ultramarathon Running | Lex Fridman Podcast #205

body.input: You know, that's just a 40 mile run, which sounds kind of silly, I think, to most people. But in perspective, we're talking about the ultra marathon running community.

metadata.title: Podcast: Zach Bitter: Ultramarathon Running | Lex Fridman Podcast #205

body.input: You know, it's a lot easier just to say like, well, you know, I'll scrap this 40 miles and try again. It's a lot harder to say I'm going to scrap the entire last four months, the entire reason why I was doing it, the countless hours I spent in there.

metadata.title: Podcast: Zach Bitter: Ultramarathon Running | Lex Fridman Podcast #205

body.input: So I think I just try to reposition it of like I'm in a bad place right now, maybe in my head or I'm not. I'm hitting a low point here, but I'm 99 percent of the way towards the goal I set out four months ago when I add in all the work I did leading up to that.

metadata.title: Podcast: Zach Bitter: Ultramarathon Running | Lex Fridman Podcast #205

body.input: So I think it's important to ask yourself why, because I mean, there are times when you're doing something and you ask yourself why and you don't have a good reason.

metadata.title: Podcast: Zach Bitter: Ultramarathon Running | Lex Fridman Podcast #205

body.input: And then maybe it is advantageous to step back and really reflect on that and decide, is this something I actually want to invest time and energy into?

metadata.title: Podcast: Zach Bitter: Ultramarathon Running | Lex Fridman Podcast #205

body.input: Because, you know, someone like yourself who is very much into a variety of different things, it can be easy probably to overextend and get, I mean, I'm a very curious person. So there's like a hundred things I would love to do if I wasn't doing what I'm doing.

metadata.title: Podcast: Zach Bitter: Ultramarathon Running | Lex Fridman Podcast #205

body.input: And I know I'd enjoy all of them. So at a certain point, though, you have to say, okay, which one is going to be the most meaningful for me?

metadata.title: Podcast: Zach Bitter: Ultramarathon Running | Lex Fridman Podcast #205

body.input: And if the answer keeps coming back to saying, I guess this is still the most meaningful to me out of that hundred things that I could otherwise be doing, then then I know that I'm in it for the right reason.

metadata.title: Podcast: Zach Bitter: Ultramarathon Running | Lex Fridman Podcast #205

body.input: And I just need to identify some of those things like, well, why did this one take the top spot out of the hundred things that I could have picked from?

metadata.title: Podcast: Zach Bitter: Ultramarathon Running | Lex Fridman Podcast #205

body.input: And keeping like a list of those in your head so that when you get to that point where you start saying, why am I doing this? Why am I here?

metadata.title: Podcast: Zach Bitter: Ultramarathon Running | Lex Fridman Podcast #205

body.input: You just have those kind of ready loaded in your head to say, well, I already took inventory on that before I started this.

metadata.title: Podcast: Zach Bitter: Ultramarathon Running | Lex Fridman Podcast #205

body.input: And I knew this voice was going to come at some point, whether it's early, middle or late.

metadata.title: Podcast: Zach Bitter: Ultramarathon Running | Lex Fridman Podcast #205

body.input: And then you just remind yourself kind of what you were thinking when you had a little more of a level head.

metadata.title: Podcast: Zach Bitter: Ultramarathon Running | Lex Fridman Podcast #205

body.input: Well, there's something about the thing you mentioned when you mentioned the death march.

metadata.title: Podcast: Zach Bitter: Ultramarathon Running | Lex Fridman Podcast #205

body.input: It seems extremely valuable to just never quitting.

metadata.title: Podcast: Zach Bitter: Ultramarathon Running | Lex Fridman Podcast #205

body.input: Like in the moment, if you decide to do something like never quitting, even if you do go through the process and realize that it's not it's not the wisest thing to be doing within the full context of your life.

metadata.title: Podcast: Zach Bitter: Ultramarathon Running | Lex Fridman Podcast #205

body.input: Like once you decide to do it, it seems like never quitting prevents you from sort of having that escape clause from other things in your life.

metadata.title: Podcast: Zach Bitter: Ultramarathon Running | Lex Fridman Podcast #205

body.input: So I've quit on a few things in my life, and I think I still deeply regret that because it opened that door.

metadata.title: Podcast: Zach Bitter: Ultramarathon Running | Lex Fridman Podcast #205

body.input: It's almost like a muscle. I don't know.

metadata.title: Podcast: Zach Bitter: Ultramarathon Running | Lex Fridman Podcast #205

body.input: So I think I'm maybe everyone is, but I think I'm kind of a quitter.

metadata.title: Podcast: Zach Bitter: Ultramarathon Running | Lex Fridman Podcast #205

body.input: You know what I mean? Like I'm really good at coming up with reasons to quit.

metadata.title: Podcast: Zach Bitter: Ultramarathon Running | Lex Fridman Podcast #205

body.input: My mind is really good at that, and I it feels like I have to come up with like really work hard to make sure that there is no quit.

metadata.title: Podcast: Zach Bitter: Ultramarathon Running | Lex Fridman Podcast #205

body.input: That never allow myself to quit, no matter how stupid the thing I'm doing is.

metadata.title: Podcast: Zach Bitter: Ultramarathon Running | Lex Fridman Podcast #205

body.input: I don't know if any of that makes sense, but it just maybe to rephrase this whole thing.

metadata.title: Podcast: Zach Bitter: Ultramarathon Running | Lex Fridman Podcast #205

body.input: Do you think it's good to live life by the ethos of never quit?

metadata.title: Podcast: Zach Bitter: Ultramarathon Running | Lex Fridman Podcast #205

body.input: Yeah, that's a really interesting thing, and I think it actually resonates with a lot of ultra marathon runners because there seems to be a trend when you have someone who's been in the sport for a long time,

metadata.title: Podcast: Zach Bitter: Ultramarathon Running | Lex Fridman Podcast #205

body.input: where there's a point where they start the sport right and they're like super excited about everything. Everything's new.

metadata.title: Podcast: Zach Bitter: Ultramarathon Running | Lex Fridman Podcast #205

body.input: It's very easy not to quit because you're like, oh, this is the first time I've ever run a 50 case, the first time ever run a 50 miles, the first time ever on 100 case, the first time ever on 100 miles and so on and so forth.

metadata.title: Podcast: Zach Bitter: Ultramarathon Running | Lex Fridman Podcast #205

body.input: And when you're doing that for the first time, I think there's a heightened motivation to not quit because you don't want your first attempt to be a failure.

metadata.title: Podcast: Zach Bitter: Ultramarathon Running | Lex Fridman Podcast #205

body.input: And then you get a little further along and you start reflecting on the landscape and all the opportunities that are out there and you find yourself quitting on an event.

metadata.title: Podcast: Zach Bitter: Ultramarathon Running | Lex Fridman Podcast #205

body.input: And there does seem to be a trend where once you do that once, now all of a sudden, like you described perfectly, that quit pops up in your head maybe a little sooner the next time or maybe a little bit before.

metadata.title: Podcast: Zach Bitter: Ultramarathon Running | Lex Fridman Podcast #205

body.input: And I've certainly had these experiences in my career as well. And what happens, I think, if you stick with it, again, I think it is important to assess whether you really want to be doing what you're doing.

metadata.title: Podcast: Zach Bitter: Ultramarathon Running | Lex Fridman Podcast #205

body.input: But if you start recognizing that about yourself in a certain activity where it's like, I think I might be pulling the plug early on some of this stuff, I think you just need to kind of get into a position where you just at that point, you need to make a decision.

metadata.title: Podcast: Zach Bitter: Ultramarathon Running | Lex Fridman Podcast #205

body.input: Do I want to keep doing this? If the answer is yes, you hold yourself accountable to not quitting.

metadata.title: Podcast: Zach Bitter: Ultramarathon Running | Lex Fridman Podcast #205

body.input: And eventually what will happen is you'll find yourself in a position where I'll use ultra marathons, for example, where you're just clicking on all cylinders for that day.

metadata.title: Podcast: Zach Bitter: Ultramarathon Running | Lex Fridman Podcast #205

body.input: And you still get those scenarios where doubt creeps in your mind, you have these low points.

metadata.title: Podcast: Zach Bitter: Ultramarathon Running | Lex Fridman Podcast #205

body.input: But for whatever reason, when those low points come, you're able to push through them better than you would have in the past.

metadata.title: Podcast: Zach Bitter: Ultramarathon Running | Lex Fridman Podcast #205

body.input: And then you push through maybe two or three more than you did after you had quit the time before.

metadata.title: Podcast: Zach Bitter: Ultramarathon Running | Lex Fridman Podcast #205

body.input: Then it's accountability time, right? Because then you have to look back at that and say, well, why did this time was I able to be mentally more strong and kind of push through those those those extra opportunities?

metadata.title: Podcast: Zach Bitter: Ultramarathon Running | Lex Fridman Podcast #205

body.input: To quit when I wasn't before. And it can be easy to look back and say and live kind of like retroactively in the sense where you're like regretting.

metadata.title: Podcast: Zach Bitter: Ultramarathon Running | Lex Fridman Podcast #205

body.input: Well, why did I drop out of those races? Why did I do this wrong there?

metadata.title: Podcast: Zach Bitter: Ultramarathon Running | Lex Fridman Podcast #205

body.input: And and that I just think that's where you have to kind of catch yourself and say, no, those those things happen to me in order to put me in a position where I decided, well, this time I'm not going to quit no matter what.

metadata.title: Podcast: Zach Bitter: Ultramarathon Running | Lex Fridman Podcast #205

body.input: You know, minus my leg falling off like I'm not going to quit. And then you put yourself in position to have that day where you push through more times than you ever have before.

metadata.title: Podcast: Zach Bitter: Ultramarathon Running | Lex Fridman Podcast #205

body.input: And you just redefine what you're capable of. And then once I think you do that, you start looking at those earlier lessons as as lessons, you know, were they failures on paper at the time?

metadata.title: Podcast: Zach Bitter: Ultramarathon Running | Lex Fridman Podcast #205

body.input: Probably. But can you pull things from them to learn as to like, well, where is your actual threshold?

metadata.title: Podcast: Zach Bitter: Ultramarathon Running | Lex Fridman Podcast #205

body.input: Where is the limit actually for you? And then kind of start redefining that stuff.

metadata.title: Podcast: Zach Bitter: Ultramarathon Running | Lex Fridman Podcast #205

body.input: So I think like the never quit mentality can be good in certain situations, but I don't think it's necessarily like a like a holistic thing where you need to be in something where it's never quit.

metadata.title: Podcast: Zach Bitter: Ultramarathon Running | Lex Fridman Podcast #205

body.input: Always do more because then you end up in a situation where you find this like margin of diminishing returns, especially when it comes to training and workouts and things like that, where there are times where often there are times where you want to.

metadata.title: Podcast: Zach Bitter: Ultramarathon Running | Lex Fridman Podcast #205

body.input: Actually quit a little bit before you would have to because the stress that was required to elicit a growth response has already occurred.

metadata.title: Podcast: Zach Bitter: Ultramarathon Running | Lex Fridman Podcast #205

body.input: And just to do more is just going to require more recovery time to get back and do it again.

metadata.title: Podcast: Zach Bitter: Ultramarathon Running | Lex Fridman Podcast #205

body.input: Yeah, this is the tricky trade off living by the never quit mentality. You're not going to achieve optimal performance in your head. You might.

metadata.title: Podcast: Zach Bitter: Ultramarathon Running | Lex Fridman Podcast #205

body.input: It seems like when you look at the full arc of human history, the people who do great things are more leaning towards the never quit.

metadata.title: Podcast: Zach Bitter: Ultramarathon Running | Lex Fridman Podcast #205

body.input: Like, I feel like at any one moment you're more in danger of quitting than you are being suboptimal.

metadata.title: Podcast: Zach Bitter: Ultramarathon Running | Lex Fridman Podcast #205

body.input: So like in terms of advice, it just feels like never quitting is always the right advice unless you deeply know the person.

metadata.title: Podcast: Zach Bitter: Ultramarathon Running | Lex Fridman Podcast #205

body.input: Maybe this is like wrestling mentality.

metadata.title: Podcast: Zach Bitter: Ultramarathon Running | Lex Fridman Podcast #205

body.input: I've seen too many and because I'm annoyed with the current culture telling me to relax and have a work life balance and all those kinds of things, which all have a deep, deep truth to them.

metadata.title: Podcast: Zach Bitter: Ultramarathon Running | Lex Fridman Podcast #205

body.input: But the reality is like there's not enough people that walk up to me and like slap me and say, get your shit together.

metadata.title: Podcast: Zach Bitter: Ultramarathon Running | Lex Fridman Podcast #205

body.input: Like, don't quit. Work harder. I think we need to hear that more.

metadata.title: Podcast: Zach Bitter: Ultramarathon Running | Lex Fridman Podcast #205

body.input: I can remember that from the wrestling rooms, like that when you're pushed that way, when you're forced to the very limit and you don't quit, that makes better humans.

metadata.title: Podcast: Zach Bitter: Ultramarathon Running | Lex Fridman Podcast #205

body.input: I think people need to get that in their life.

metadata.title: Podcast: Zach Bitter: Ultramarathon Running | Lex Fridman Podcast #205

body.input: I think they need to have situations where that becomes kind of the reality for them so they can see that avenue, experience that avenue, where I think it's maybe to the extreme as if it becomes like your entire life philosophy where like every little thing you do is never quit.

metadata.title: Podcast: Zach Bitter: Ultramarathon Running | Lex Fridman Podcast #205

body.input: But life is short, Zach.

metadata.title: Podcast: Zach Bitter: Ultramarathon Running | Lex Fridman Podcast #205

body.input: Like why? I mean, this is the problem I have.

metadata.title: Podcast: Zach Bitter: Ultramarathon Running | Lex Fridman Podcast #205

body.input: This is probably the programming thing too is over optimization is dangerous.

metadata.title: Podcast: Zach Bitter: Ultramarathon Running | Lex Fridman Podcast #205

body.input: It's like every once in a while.

metadata.title: Podcast: Zach Bitter: Ultramarathon Running | Lex Fridman Podcast #205

body.input: I mean, you're you do this kind of stuff.

metadata.title: Podcast: Zach Bitter: Ultramarathon Running | Lex Fridman Podcast #205

body.input: You're not, for example, with 100 mile run.

metadata.title: Podcast: Zach Bitter: Ultramarathon Running | Lex Fridman Podcast #205

body.input: You're I mean, you could just be doing that for the rest of your life and do like the most optimal 100 mile run ever.

metadata.title: Podcast: Zach Bitter: Ultramarathon Running | Lex Fridman Podcast #205

body.input: But you keep taking on like new challenges and there's a lot more chaos in that.

metadata.title: Podcast: Zach Bitter: Ultramarathon Running | Lex Fridman Podcast #205

body.input: And there it feels like the muscle of never quit will be much more important than the optimality of your training.

metadata.title: Podcast: Zach Bitter: Ultramarathon Running | Lex Fridman Podcast #205

body.input: Yeah, so there's probably a couple sides to me with that kind of a thing where for one, I think when we talked about the why.

metadata.title: Podcast: Zach Bitter: Ultramarathon Running | Lex Fridman Podcast #205

body.input: So like I think the why can kind of shift a bit and it probably will if you do something long enough or evolve maybe is a better way to put it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Zach Bitter: Ultramarathon Running | Lex Fridman Podcast #205

body.input: And for me, like one of my big drives and one of my big passions within ultra running is to first of all, find an event that I really, really love to train for and participate in.

metadata.title: Podcast: Zach Bitter: Ultramarathon Running | Lex Fridman Podcast #205

body.input: So for me, I feel like I've kind of identified it to a degree and that's kind of runnable hundred milers.

metadata.title: Podcast: Zach Bitter: Ultramarathon Running | Lex Fridman Podcast #205

body.input: So once I found that it became more of a driver for me to see like, well, how fast can I run 100 miles in a very controlled environment?

metadata.title: Podcast: Zach Bitter: Ultramarathon Running | Lex Fridman Podcast #205

body.input: So let's eliminate weather, let's eliminate elevation, let's eliminate like having to wait extra long to get crew or support and that sort of thing.

metadata.title: Podcast: Zach Bitter: Ultramarathon Running | Lex Fridman Podcast #205

body.input: And that's how you find yourself on a 400 meter track running 100 miles.

metadata.title: Podcast: Zach Bitter: Ultramarathon Running | Lex Fridman Podcast #205

body.input: But for me, like that, the important part of that is that I can control the environment enough where if I come back year after year, I can retest myself and have a decent ability to kind of say I improved or I regressed or I stayed stagnant.

metadata.title: Podcast: Zach Bitter: Ultramarathon Running | Lex Fridman Podcast #205

body.input: And I think that's a big driver for me.

metadata.title: Podcast: Zach Bitter: Ultramarathon Running | Lex Fridman Podcast #205

body.input: But one thing I've recognized within that is if you just keep doing that, like if I could probably pick three flat runnable hundred milers a year and optimally prepare, race, recover and repeat without like burning myself out.

metadata.title: Podcast: Zach Bitter: Ultramarathon Running | Lex Fridman Podcast #205

body.input: But one thing I think I learned also in 2019 was that sometimes you kind of need to step away from some of these really, really kind of important markers in your like your performance or in whatever you're trying to do and take a step away from it and try to do something a little different in order to kind of hit the reset button on just like what I would call just like your mental energy to be able to continue to do it at a high level.

metadata.title: Podcast: Zach Bitter: Ultramarathon Running | Lex Fridman Podcast #205

body.input: So almost like happiness. Exactly. Well, and here's the example. Like, I mean, I love running in trails to most people would consider me a flat road track runner, runnable ultra runner.

metadata.title: Podcast: Zach Bitter: Ultramarathon Running | Lex Fridman Podcast #205

body.input: But I like to do trail runs too. So and at the end of 2018, I recognized that I had been kind of pushing the gas pedal on trying to run fast hundred milers for quite a while without really a break in that where it was like, OK, I did one.

metadata.title: Podcast: Zach Bitter: Ultramarathon Running | Lex Fridman Podcast #205

body.input: Now I'm going to take a brief off season, but then I'm going to ultimately build up and peak for another one. I might introduce some fun trail races in the context, but they're going to be races are going to be training races, time on feet type of stuff that are going to kind of mimic like a long run essentially.

metadata.title: Podcast: Zach Bitter: Ultramarathon Running | Lex Fridman Podcast #205

body.input: And but the main focus, the always in the back of my mind was like getting on the track and seeing how much faster I can run 100 miles. And that just kind of that energy that it takes to continually think by that that I think the motivation to keep that stoke high enough to really meet your full potential.

metadata.title: Podcast: Zach Bitter: Ultramarathon Running | Lex Fridman Podcast #205

body.input: And it's a lot of aids if you don't step away from it for a little bit. So I took essentially half a year away from runnable stuff and just decided I'm going to prepare for the San Diego 100 mile, which is like much more elevation, technical trail type of an event.

metadata.title: Podcast: Zach Bitter: Ultramarathon Running | Lex Fridman Podcast #205

body.input: Yeah, it's a trail 100 miler actually just kind of just outside of San Diego. And yeah, it goes through. It goes over part of the Pacific Crest Trail and stuff. So it's very different than running on a runnable surface. So to give you some context, like I ran, I think just under 17 hours for that race, whereas on a flat surface, I can run 11 hours and 19 minutes.

metadata.title: Podcast: Zach Bitter: Ultramarathon Running | Lex Fridman Podcast #205

body.input: So just the environment alone added an extra five plus hours to the day. So it's just a different experience, different skill set. And what it did is it allowed me to kind of step away from kind of focusing on like splits on a track, running flat stuff, like preparing for things specifically for a flat

metadata.title: Podcast: Zach Bitter: Ultramarathon Running | Lex Fridman Podcast #205

body.input: environment and start training for something that's more climbing and descending, more technical running skill sets and things like that. And the cool part about it was, first of all, when you step away from something and enter something a lot different, I mean, it's still running.

metadata.title: Podcast: Zach Bitter: Ultramarathon Running | Lex Fridman Podcast #205

body.input: There's still a huge advantage I had from the running I had done in the past that was going to put me in a good position to be successful. But there was a much higher or much bigger range of potential improvement for me.

metadata.title: Podcast: Zach Bitter: Ultramarathon Running | Lex Fridman Podcast #205

body.input: So through the four plus months I spent preparing for that race, I noticed, oh, wow, I'm getting faster on this climb, or I'm getting better at descending this technical trail. It was one of the most fun races I've run, actually. So it was kind of a cool experience.

metadata.title: Podcast: Zach Bitter: Ultramarathon Running | Lex Fridman Podcast #205

body.input: I ended up taking the lead at like 93 miles. So you were racing, racing, like you were trying to get first. So it's still a race. Yeah. So what was the enjoyable aspect of it?

metadata.title: Podcast: Zach Bitter: Ultramarathon Running | Lex Fridman Podcast #205

body.input: I don't think I recognized it so much while I was doing it, actually. It surfaced afterwards. I mean, the enjoyment of the race itself is like when you find yourself in a position where you're sitting in basically second place all day long, and then you take the lead at 90, I think it was like 91 or 92 miles.

metadata.title: Podcast: Zach Bitter: Ultramarathon Running | Lex Fridman Podcast #205

body.input: It's like, yeah, that's kind of a cool way to race.

metadata.title: Podcast: Zach Bitter: Ultramarathon Running | Lex Fridman Podcast #205

body.input: But afterwards I recognized a few things just about kind of pacing and how to maybe pace the first half of 100-miler versus the second half. metadata.title: Podcast: Zach Bitter: Ultramarathon Running | Lex Fridman Podcast #205

body.input: And I don't think that would have been the case had I just tried to do another flat, fast 100-miler earlier or during that year and end up in a situation where I maybe had normalized a suboptimal outlook on something that I had just done so many times already.

metadata.title: Podcast: Zach Bitter: Ultramarathon Running | Lex Fridman Podcast #205

body.input: And I recognize that just every workout I did, I was like, I did this workout a year ago and it was not nearly this much fun. And then the interesting thing about these track hundreds too is like you find yourself doing like your peaking phase where you're running your long runs, which for me are usually like around 30 miles or so and I'll do them on back to back days.

metadata.title: Podcast: Zach Bitter: Ultramarathon Running | Lex Fridman Podcast #205

body.input: And I try to replicate the environment I'm going to race on. So I find myself on a 400-meter track. And it's like when I started doing that again, I just felt like I was super motivated to go out there Saturday and Sunday and do those back to back long runs and see the progress and then head out again the next week and do it again.

metadata.title: Podcast: Zach Bitter: Ultramarathon Running | Lex Fridman Podcast #205

body.input: So I had some of my more enjoyable long runs, which are going to be the most specific to race day environment that I had in quite some time. And I think that was really beneficial and kind of putting me in the right spot to be able to push through barriers on race day and put me in a position where quitting was going to be much less of a likelihood given the enjoyment I had in the months leading into the race itself.

metadata.title: Podcast: Zach Bitter: Ultramarathon Running | Lex Fridman Podcast #205

body.input: Yeah, even the thought of quitting. Yeah. So you mentioned the track. You've also ran a hundred miles in the treadmill and the trail hundred mile broadly. If we zoom out, what does it take to run a hundred miles for most of the world?

metadata.title: Podcast: Zach Bitter: Ultramarathon Running | Lex Fridman Podcast #205

body.input: That seems like a crazy distance to run. So maybe it's interesting to ask not only is just setting the world record, but purely running. What does it take to run that far?

metadata.title: Podcast: Zach Bitter: Ultramarathon Running | Lex Fridman Podcast #205

body.input: Yeah. I mean, I think people probably overestimate what it takes in terms of just getting it done. I think this is consistent in just running in general. I think the marathon was always a big one with that where people thought like, well, you have to do this training or you just literally won't physically be able to complete a marathon.

metadata.title: Podcast: Zach Bitter: Ultramarathon Running | Lex Fridman Podcast #205

body.input: And then we got into an era of kind of like running as more of an enjoyment thing versus a performance thing. And then you'd have people running granted much slower. I think if you look at the Boston marathon average finishing times, it goes from like, or maybe it wasn't the Boston marathon.

metadata.title: Podcast: Zach Bitter: Ultramarathon Running | Lex Fridman Podcast #205

body.input: I might've just been marathons in general went from like three hours to five hours or something like that. So it's like people I think got past the fact that you can only do it if you're optimally prepared to, well, I can do it and maybe not meet my full potential.

metadata.title: Podcast: Zach Bitter: Ultramarathon Running | Lex Fridman Podcast #205

body.input: If I'm going to like not do much training, which I wouldn't necessarily advise, but I mean, I've talked to people who basically run a hundred miles sometimes almost off the couch. And it's like, it's to me, what that says is just the human body is incredible and what it can tolerate above and beyond what it's been exposed to if it has to, or if it feels like it has to.

metadata.title: Podcast: Zach Bitter: Ultramarathon Running | Lex Fridman Podcast #205

body.input: So that's the basic sort of getting from point A from the start to the finish. It's the human body and the human mind is capable of doing it without much preparation. But then you start to increase the goal of performance and you try to get to actually a good, like the most out of your body that you can.

metadata.title: Podcast: Zach Bitter: Ultramarathon Running | Lex Fridman Podcast #205

body.input: How does that start to change then? Going from fun to performance? Yeah, I think once you start putting marks or goals on outside of just finishing, that's where it starts getting interesting. Because now you can maybe go in with multiple goals where like if one falls off due to something that you didn't expect, then you have another one to target.

metadata.title: Podcast: Zach Bitter: Ultramarathon Running | Lex Fridman Podcast #205

body.input: But you can always build those up and try to think like, well, I want to run faster than last time, or I want to break a course record or an age group record or something like that. And that I think is just going to be a little bit of a different mindset because now you're looking at every little thing from what do I need to do to prepare as well as what do I need to do to be efficient on the day itself?

metadata.title: Podcast: Zach Bitter: Ultramarathon Running | Lex Fridman Podcast #205

body.input: So like transitioning aid stations and things like that, or do I want to pace or not? Or does this race allow someone to like hand me a bottle at a certain spot or do I have to be in specific areas to get that type of stuff?

metadata.title: Podcast: Zach Bitter: Ultramarathon Running | Lex Fridman Podcast #205

body.input: And what it ends up doing is it ends up bringing a lot more variables to the table. And I think it's interesting because there's always going to be more variables on the day than you are able to account for. So at a certain degree, you have to kind of find yourself in a position where I'm going to make sure I take care of the big ones or the ones that are like, obviously, I need to be ready for like my fueling strategy, my hydration strategy, my pacing strategy, what workouts are going to put me in a position to physiologically have that

metadata.title: Podcast: Zach Bitter: Ultramarathon Running | Lex Fridman Podcast #205

body.input: this process go as well as possible? How am I going to like, you know, hold myself accountable in aid station transition so I'm not like having a ton of non moving time versus moving time and things like that.

metadata.title: Podcast: Zach Bitter: Ultramarathon Running | Lex Fridman Podcast #205

body.input: So cool. So there's these like big variables that you're aware of and you're trying to optimize over this space of variables. So you get to start to play with that when you're looking for performance.

metadata.title: Podcast: Zach Bitter: Ultramarathon Running | Lex Fridman Podcast #205

body.input: It's almost like moving from checkers to chess, right? You have like, or maybe even like connect forward to chess or something like that, where it goes from just kind of like, well, one foot in front of the other. And when I get to the next aid station, I'll just eat whatever looks good, drink whatever, you know, quenches my thirst and then move on to the next one to like, well, which one of these food products is actually going to make me move a little faster the next aid station or, you know, which one of these pacing strategies is going to get me to the finish line faster than the other one and that sort of stuff.

metadata.title: Podcast: Zach Bitter: Ultramarathon Running | Lex Fridman Podcast #205

body.input: So it gets more complicated, more interesting. And in my opinion, anyway, also, there's I mean, but there's a breaking point with that, too, because, like I said, there's an endless number of variables you could account for.

metadata.title: Podcast: Zach Bitter: Ultramarathon Running | Lex Fridman Podcast #205

body.input: And as the distance gets longer, that list gets longer, too. So you find yourself in this position where where you have to at some point say, OK, I've accounted for everything I can reasonably account for.

metadata.title: Podcast: Zach Bitter: Ultramarathon Running | Lex Fridman Podcast #205

body.input: Now I need to be in a mental space where when something happens that I wasn't able to account for, I'm able to respond to it with the right decision and keep going and not dwell on it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Zach Bitter: Ultramarathon Running | Lex Fridman Podcast #205

metadata.title: Podcast: Zach Bitter: Ultramarathon Running | Lex Fridman Podcast #205

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: to. Efficiency and reliability. Reliability. You have to get both. What's reliability?
