body.input: I really want my telephone calls to get through and I want the quality of what I am talking,

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: coming out at the other end. The other end might be in London or wherever. And you don't want the

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: system to be crashing. If you're doing a bank, you mustn't crash. It might be your bank account

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: that is in trouble. There's different constraints like in games, it doesn't matter too much if

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: there's a crash, nobody dies and nobody gets ruined. But I'm interested in the combination

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: of performance, partly because of sort of speed of things being done, part of being able to do

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: things that is necessary to have reliability of larger systems. If you spend all your time

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: interpreting a simple function call, you are not going to have enough time to do proper

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: signal processing to get the telephone calls to sound right. Either that or you have to have 10

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: times as many computers and you can't afford your phone anymore. It's a ridiculous idea

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: in the modern world because we have solved all of those problems.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: I mean, they keep popping up in different ways because we tackle bigger and bigger problems,

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: so efficiency remains always an important aspect. But you have to think about efficiency,

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: not just as speed, but as an enabler to important things. And one of the things it enables is

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: reliability, is dependability. When I press the pedal, the brake pedal of a car,

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: it is not actually connected directly to anything but a computer. That computer better work.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: Let's talk about reliability just a little bit. So modern cars have ECUs, have millions of lines

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: of code today. So this is certainly especially true of autonomous vehicles where some of the

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: aspects of the control or driver assistance systems that steer the car, that keep it in the lane,

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: and so on. So how do you think, you know, I talked to regulators, people in government,

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: who are very nervous about testing the safety of these systems of software, ultimately software

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: that makes decisions that could lead to fatalities. So how do we test software systems like these?

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: First of all, safety, like performance and like security, is a systems property. People tend to

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: look at one part of a system at a time and saying something like, this is secure. That's all right.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: I don't need to do that. Yeah, that piece of code is secure. I'll buy your operator.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: Right. If you want to have reliability, if you want to have performance, if you want to have

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: security, you have to look at the whole system. I did not expect you to say that, but that's very

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: true. Yes. I'm dealing with one part of the system and I want my part to be really good,

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: but I know it's not the whole system. Furthermore, making an individual part perfect

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: may actually not be the best way of getting the highest degree of reliability and performance

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: and such. There's people who say C++ is type safe, not type safe. You can break it. Sure,

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: sure. I can break anything that runs on a computer. I may not go through your type system.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: If I wanted to break into your computer, I'll probably try SQL injection.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: It's very true. If you think about safety or even reliability at a system level,

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: especially when a human being is involved, it starts becoming hopeless pretty quickly in terms of

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: proving that something is safe to a certain level. Yeah. Because there's so many variables. It's so

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: complex. Well, let's get back to something we can talk about and actually make some progress on.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: Yes. We can look at C++ programs and we can try and make sure they crash less often.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: The way you do that is largely by simplification. The first step is to simplify the code, have less

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: code, have code that are less likely to go wrong. It's not by runtime testing everything. It is not

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: by big test frameworks that you're using. Yes, we do that also, but the first step is actually to

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: make sure that when you want to express something, you can express it directly in code rather than

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: going through endless loops and convolutions in your head before it gets down the code.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: If the way you're thinking about a problem is not in the code, there is a missing piece that's just

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: in your head and the code you can see what it does, but it cannot see what you thought about it

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: unless you have expressed things directly. When you express things directly, you can maintain it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: It's easier to find errors. It's easier to make modifications. It's actually easier to test it

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: and lo and behold, it runs faster. Therefore, you can use a smaller algorithm to make it

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: run faster. You can use a smaller number of computers, which means there's less hardware

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: that could possibly break. I think the key here is simplification, but it has to be,

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: to use the Einstein quote, as simple as possible and no simpler.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: Not simpler.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: There are other areas with under constraints where you can be simpler than you can be in C++,

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: but the things that I'm dealing with, that's the simplification I'm after.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: How do you inspire or ensure that the Einstein level of simplification is reached?

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: Can you do code review? Can you look at code? If I gave you the code for the Ford F-150

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: and said, here, is this a mess or is this okay? Is it possible to tell? Is it possible to regulate?

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: An experienced developer can look at code and see if it smells.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: I mixed metaphors deliberately. The point is that

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: it is hard to generate something that is really obviously clean and

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: can be appreciated, but you can usually recognize when you haven't reached that point.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: I've never looked at the F-150 code, so I wouldn't know, but I know what I ought to be looking at.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: I'll be looking for some tricks that correlate with bugs and elsewhere.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: I have tried to formulate rules for what good code looks like.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: The current version of that is called the C++ core guidelines.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: One thing people should remember is there's what you can do in a language.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: What you can do in a language and what you should do.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: In a language, you have lots of things that is necessary in some contexts, but not in others.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: There's things that exist just because there's 30-year-old code out there and you can't get

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: rid of it, but you can't have rules that says when you create it, try and follow these rules.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: This does not create good programs by themselves, but it limits the damage

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: and for mistakes, it limits the possibilities of mistakes.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: And basically, we are trying to say what is it that a good programmer does

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: at the fairly simple level of where you use the language and how you use it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: Now, I can put all the rules for chiseling in Marlboro.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: It doesn't mean that somebody who follows all of those rules can do a masterpiece by Michelangelo.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: That is, there's something else to write a good program, just is there something else to create

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: an important work of art that is some kind of inspiration, understanding, gift.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: But we can approach the sort of technical, the craftsmanship level of it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: The famous painters, the famous sculptures was among other things,

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: superb craftsmen. They could express their ideas using their tools very well.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: And so these days, I think what I'm doing, what a lot of people are doing,

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: we are still trying to figure out how it is to use our tools very well.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: For a really good piece of code, you need a spark of inspiration and you can't, I think, regulate that.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: You cannot say that I'll take a picture only, I'll buy your picture only if you're at least Van Gogh.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: There are other things you can regulate, but not the inspiration.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: I think that's quite beautifully put. It is true that there is, as an experienced programmer,

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: when you see code that's inspired, that's like Michelangelo, you know it when you see it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: And the opposite of that is code that is messy, code that smells, you know when you see it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: And I'm not sure you can describe it in words, except vaguely through guidelines and so on.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: Yes, it's easier to recognize ugly than to recognize beauty in code. And for the reason is that sometimes

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: beauty comes from something that's innovative and unusual. And you have to sometimes think reasonably

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: hard to appreciate that. On the other hand, the messes have things in common. And you can have

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: static checkers and dynamic checkers that finds a large number of the most common mistakes.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: You can catch a lot of sloppiness mechanically. I'm a great fan of static analysis in particular,

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: because you can check for not just the language rules, but for the usage of language rules.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: And I think we will see much more static analysis in the coming decade.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: Can you describe what static analysis is?

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: You represent a piece of code so that you can write a program that goes over that representation

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: and look for things that are right and not right. So for instance, you can

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: analyze a program to see if resources are leaked. That's one of my favorite problems. It's

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: not actually all that hard in modern C++, but you can do it. If you are writing in the C level,

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: you have to have a malloc and a free, and they have to match. If you have them in a single function,

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: you can usually do it very easily. If there's a malloc here, there should be a free there.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: On the other hand, in between can be showing complete code and then it becomes impossible.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: If you pass that pointer to the memory out of a function and then want to make sure that the free

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: is done somewhere else, now it gets really difficult. And so for static analysis,

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: you can run through a program and you can try and figure out if there's any leaks.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: And what you will probably find is that you will find some leaks and you'll find quite a few

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: places where your analysis can't be complete. It might depend on runtime. It might depend on

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: the cleverness of your analyzer. And it might take a long time. Some of these programs run for a long

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: time, but if you combine such analysis with a set of rules, it says how people could use it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: You can actually see why the rules are violated and that stops you from getting into the impossible

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: complexities. You don't want to solve the holding problem. The static analysis is looking at the

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: code without running the code. Yes. And thereby it's almost not a production code, but it's almost

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: like an educational tool of how the language should be used. It guides you like it at its best,

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: right? It would guide you in how you write future code as well and you learn together. Yes. So

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: basically you need a set of rules for how you use the language. Then you need a static analysis

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: that catches your mistakes when you violate the rules or when your code ends up doing things that

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: it shouldn't despite the rules, because there is the language rules. We can go further. And

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: again, it's back to my idea that I would much rather find errors before I start running the code.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: If nothing else, once the code runs, if it catches an error at run times, I have to have an error

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: handler. And one of the hardest things to write in code is error handling code, because you know

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: something went wrong. Do you know really exactly what went wrong? Usually not. But you can't

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: be 100% sure what the problem was in many, many cases. And this is part of it. So yes,

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: we need good languages, we need good type systems, we need rules for how to use them,

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: we need static analysis. And the ultimate for static analysis is of course program proof,

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: but that still doesn't scale to the level of the code that you're using. So you need to have a

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: good type of system, but that still doesn't scale to the kind of systems we deploy. Then we start

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: needing testing and the rest of the stuff. So C++ is an object-oriented programming language

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: that creates, especially with its newer versions, as we'll talk about, higher and higher levels of

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: abstraction. So how do you design, let's even go back to the origin of C++, how do you design

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: abstraction that's still efficient and is still something that you can manage, do static analysis

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: on, you can have constraints on, they can be reliable, all those things we've talked about.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: So to me, there's a slight tension between high level abstraction and efficiency.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: That's a good question. I could probably have a year's course, just trying to answer it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: Yes, there's a tension between efficiency and abstraction, but you also get the interesting

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: situation that you get the best efficiency out of the best abstraction. And my main tool

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: for efficiency for performance actually is abstraction. So let's go back to how C++ got

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: there. You said it was object-oriented programming language. I actually never said that.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: It's always quoted, but I never did. I said C++ supports object-oriented programming and other

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: techniques. And that's important because I think that the best solution to most

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: complex, interesting problems require ideas and techniques from things that has been called

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: object-oriented data abstraction, functional, traditional C-style code, all of the above.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: And so when I was designing C++, I soon realized I couldn't just add features

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: if you just add what looks pretty or what people ask for or what you think is good.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: One by one, you're not going to get a coherent whole. What you need is a set of guidelines that

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: guide your decisions. Should this feature be in or should this feature be out? How should a feature

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: be modified before it can go in and such? And in the book I wrote about that, the design and

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: evolution of C++, there's a whole bunch of rules like that. Most of them are not language technical.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: They are things like, don't violate static type system because I like static type system

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: for the obvious reason that I like things to be reliable on reasonable amounts of hardware.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: But one of these rules is the zero overhead principle.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: What kind of principle?

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: The zero overhead principle. It basically says that if you have an abstraction,

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: it should not cost anything compared to write the equivalent code at a lower level.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: So if I have, say, a matrix multiply, it should be written in such a way that you could not

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: drop to the C level abstraction and use arrays and pointers and such and run faster.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: And so people have written such matrix multiplications and they've actually gotten

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: code that ran faster than Fortran because once you had the right abstraction, you can eliminate

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: temporaries and you can do loop fusion and other good stuff like that that's quite hard to do by

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: hand and in a lower level language. And there's some really nice examples of that.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: And the key here is that that matrix multiplication, the matrix abstraction allows

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: you to write code that's simple and easy. You can do that in any language, but with C++,

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: it has the features so that you can also have this thing run faster than if you hand coded it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: Now, people have given that lecture many times, I and others, and are very common on

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: a question after the talk where you have demonstrated that you can outperform Fortran

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: for dense matrix multiplication. People come up and say, yeah, but there are C++.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: If I rewrote your code and see how much faster would it run? The answer is much slower.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: This happened the first time actually back in the 80s with a friend of mine called Doug McElroy,

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: who demonstrated exactly this effect. And so the principle is you should give programmers the tools

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: so that the abstractions can follow the zero-weight principle. Furthermore, when you put in a language

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: feature in C++ or a standard library feature, you try to meet this. It doesn't mean it's absolutely

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: optimal, but it means if you hand code it with the usual facilities in the language in C++, in C,

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: you should not be able to better it. Usually you can do better if you use embedded assembler

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: for machine code for some of the details to utilize part of a computer that the compiler

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: doesn't know about. But you should get to that point before you beat the abstraction.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: So that's a beautiful ideal to reach for. And we meet it quite often.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: Quite often. So where's the magic of that coming from? Some of it is the compilation process, so

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: the implementation of C++. Some of it is the design of the feature itself, the guidelines,

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: so I've recently and often talked to Chris Latner, so Clang. Just out of curiosity, is your

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: relationship in general with the different implementations in C++, as you think about you

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: and committee and other people in C++, think about the design of new features or design of previous

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: features, what are the things that you're going to be able to do in the future?

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: In trying to reach the ideal of zero overhead, does the magic come from the design, the guidelines,

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: or from the implementations? And not all. You go for programming technique,

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: programming language features, and implementation techniques. You need all three.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: And how can you think about all three at the same time?

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: It takes some experience, it takes some practice, and sometimes you get it wrong, but after a while

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: you sort of get it right. I don't write compilers anymore, but Brian Kernahan pointed out that one

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: of the reasons C++ succeeded was some of the craftsmanship I put into the early compilers.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: And of course I did the language design, and of course I wrote a fair amount of code using

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: this kind of stuff. And I think most of the successes involve progress in all three areas

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: together. A small group of people can do that. Two, three people can work together to do something

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: like that. It's ideal if it's one person that has all the skills necessary, but nobody has all the

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: skills necessary in all the fields where C++ is used. So if you want to approach my ideal in,

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: say, concurrent programming, you need to know about algorithms from concurrent programming.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: You need to know the trigger of lock-free programming. You need to know something about

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: compiler techniques, and then you have to know some of the application areas where this is,

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: like some forms of graphics or some forms of what we call web serving kind of stuff.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: And that's very hard to get into a single head, but small groups can do it too.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: So is there differences in your view, not saying which is better or so on, but differences in the

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: different implementations of C++? Why are there several sort of maybe naive questions for me?

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: GCC, Clang, so on?

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: This is a very reasonable question. When I designed C++,

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: most languages had multiple implementations because if you want an IBM, if you run on a Sun,

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: if you want a Motorola, there was just many, many companies and they each have their own

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: compilation structure and their own compilers. It was just fairly common that there was many of them.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: And I wrote Cfront assuming that other people would write compilers with C++ if I was successful.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: And furthermore, I wanted to utilize all the backend infrastructures that were available.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: I soon realized that my users were using 25 different linkers. I couldn't write my own linker.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: Yes, I could, but I couldn't write 25 linkers and also get any work done on the language.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: And so it came from a world where there was many linkers, many optimizers, many compiler front ends,

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: not to start, but many operating systems. The whole world was not an 86 and a Linux box or

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: something, whatever is the standard today. In the old days, they said a set of X. So basically,

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: I assumed there would be lots of compilers. It was not a decision that there should be many compilers.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: It was just a fact. That's the way the world is. And yes, many compilers emerged and today

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: there's at least four front ends, Clang, GCC, Microsoft, and EDG. It is the same group.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: They supply a lot of the independent organizations and the embedded systems industry.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: And there's lots and lots of backends. We have to think about how many dozen backends there are.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: Because different machines have different things, especially in the embedded world,

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: the machines are very different. The architectures are very different. And so having a single

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: implementation was never an option. Now, I also happen to dislike monocultures. Monocultures.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: They are dangerous because whoever owns the monoculture can go stale and there's no competition

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: and there's no incentive to innovate. There's a lot of incentive to put barriers in the way of

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: change because, hey, we own the world and it's a very comfortable world for us. And who are you to

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: mess with that? So I really am very happy that there's four front ends for C++. Clang's great,

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: but GCC was great. But then it got somewhat stale. Clang came along and GCC is much better now.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: Competition is good.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: Microsoft is much better now. So at least a low number of front end puts a lot of pressure on

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: standards compliance and also on performance and error messages and compile time speed,

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: all this good stuff that we want.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: Do you think crazy questions like this are going to be answered?

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: I think there might come along implementation of C++ written given all of its history written from

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: scratch. So written today from scratch.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: Well, Clang and the LLVM is more or less written from scratch.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: But there's been C plus plus 11, 14, 17, 20, you know, there's been a lot of

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: sooner or later, somebody is going to try again.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: There has been attempts to write new C plus plus compilers and some of them

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: has been used and some of them has been absorbed into others and such.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: Yeah, it'll happen.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: So what are the key features of C plus plus?

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: And let's use that as a way to serve, talk about the evolution of C plus plus,

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: the new feature.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: So at the highest level, what are the features that were there in the

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: beginning and what features got added?

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: Let's first get a principle or an aim in place.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: C plus plus is for people who want to use hardware really well and then manage the

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: complexity of doing that through abstraction.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: And so the first facility you have is a way of manipulating the machines at a

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: fairly low level.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: That looks very much like C.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: It has loops, it has variables, it has pointers like machine addresses.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: It can access memory directly.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: It can allocate stuff in the absolute minimum of space needed on the machine.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: There's a machine facing part of C plus plus, which is roughly equivalent to C.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: I said C plus plus could beat C and it can.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: Doesn't mean I dislike C.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: If I disliked C, I wouldn't have built on it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: Furthermore, after Dennis Ritchie, I'm probably the major contributor to

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: modern C. And well, I had lunch with Dennis most days for 16 years and we

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: never had a harsh word between us.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: So these C versus C plus plus fights are for people who don't quite

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: understand what's going on.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: Then the other part is the abstraction.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: And there the key is the class, which is a user defined type.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: And my idea for the class is that you should be able to build a type that's

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: just like the built in types in the way you use them, in the way you declare

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: them, in the way you get the memory and you can do just as well.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: So in C plus plus as an int, as in C, you should be able to build an

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: abstraction, a class, which we can call capital int.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: That you can use exactly like an integer and run just as fast as an integer.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: There's the idea right there.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: And of course you probably don't want to use the int itself, but it has happened.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: People have wanted integers that were range checked so that you couldn't

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: overflow and such, especially for very safety critical applications like the

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: fuel injection for a Marine diesel engine for the largest ships.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: This is a real example, by the way, this has been done.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: They built themselves an integer that was just like integer, except

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: that it couldn't overflow.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: If there was an overflow, you went into the error handling.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: And then you built more interesting types.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: You can build a matrix, which you need to do graphics, or you could

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: build a gnome for a video game.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: And all of these are classes and they appear just like the built-in types.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: Exactly.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: In terms of efficiency and so on.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: So what else is there?

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: And flexibility.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: So, I don't know, for people who are not familiar with object oriented

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: programming, there's inheritance.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: There's a hierarchy of classes.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: You can just like you said, create a generic vehicle that can turn left.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: So what people found was that you don't actually know.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: How do I say this?

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: A lot of types are related.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: That is the vehicles, all vehicles are related.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: Bicycles, cars, fire engines, tanks.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: They have some things in common and some things that differ.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: And you would like to have the common things common and having the

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: differences specific, and when you didn't want to know about the

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: differences, like just turn left.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: You don't have to worry about it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: That's how you get the traditional object oriented programming coming out

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: of Simula adopted by small talk and C++ and all the other languages.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: The other kind of obvious similarity between types comes when you

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: have something like a vector.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: Fortran gave us the vector called array of doubles.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: But the minute you have a vector of doubles, you want a vector of double

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: precision doubles and for short doubles for graphics and why should you

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: have not have a vector of integers while you're added or vector of vectors

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: and a vector of vectors of chess pieces.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: Now you have a board, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: So this is you express the commonality as the idea of a vector and the

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: variations come through parameterization.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: And so here we get the two fundamental ways of abstracting or of having

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: similarities of types in C++.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: There's the inheritance and there's a parameterization.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: There's the object oriented programming and there's the generic programming.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: What was the, why didn't it, what, like what, we'll talk a little bit about this

body.input: fascinating process of standards because I think it's really interesting for people.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: It's interesting for me, but why did it take so long?

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: What shapes did the idea of concepts take?

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: What were the challenges?

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: Back in 87 or thereabouts, 1987, 1987 or thereabouts when I was designing templates,

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: obviously I wanted to express the notion of what is required by a

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: template of its arguments.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: And so I looked at this and basically for templates, I wanted three properties.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: I wanted to be very flexible.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: It had to be able to express things I couldn't imagine because I know I can't

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: imagine everything and I've been suffering from languages and tried to

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: constrain you to only do what you're the designer thought good.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: Didn't want to do that.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: Secondly, it had to run faster as fast or faster than handwritten code.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: So basically if I have a vector of T and I take a vector of child, I

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: have a vector of char, it should run as fast as you build a vector of char

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: yourself without parameterization.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: And second, and thirdly, I wanted to be able to express the constraints of.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: Of the arguments have proper type checking of the interfaces and neither

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: I know anybody else at the time knew how to get all three.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: And I thought for C plus plus, I must have the two first.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: Otherwise it's not C plus plus.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: And it bothered me for another couple of decades that I couldn't solve the third

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: one.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: I mean, I was the one that put function argument type checking into C.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: I know the value of good interfaces.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: I didn't invent that idea.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: It's very common, but I did it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: And I wanted to do the same for templates, of course.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: And I couldn't, so it bothered me.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: Then we tried again, 2002, 2003, Kevin, as raised, and I started analyzing the

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: problem, explained possible solutions.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: There was not a complete design.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: A group in university of Indiana, an old friend of mine, they started a project at

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: Indiana and we thought we could get a good system of concepts in another two or

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: three years that would have made C plus plus 11 to C plus plus 06 or 07.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: Well, it, it turns out that I think we got a lot of the fundamental ideas,

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: wrong.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: They were too conventional.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: They didn't quite fit C plus plus, in my opinion, didn't serve implicit

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: conversions very well.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: It didn't serve mixed type arithmetic, mixed type computations very well.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: A lot of stuff came out of the functional community and it, that community

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: didn't deal with multiple types in the same way as C plus plus does, had more

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: constraints on, on what you could express and didn't have the draconian

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: performance requirements.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: And basically we tried, we tried very hard.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: We had some successes, but it just in the end wasn't, didn't compile fast

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: enough, was too hard.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: To use and didn't run fast enough unless you had optimizers that was beyond

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: the state of the art.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: They still are.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: So we had to do something else.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: Basically it was the idea that a set of parameters has defined a set of

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: operations and you go through an indirection table, just like for virtual

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: functions, and then you try to do something else.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: And then you try to optimize the interaction away to get performance.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: And we just couldn't do all of that.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: But get back to the standardization.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: We are standardizing C plus plus under ISO rules, which are very open process.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: People come in, there's no requirements for education or experience.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: So you've started to develop C plus plus and there's a whole, what was the

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: first standard established?

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: What is that like?

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: The ISO standard, is there a committee that you're referring to?

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: There's a group of people.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: What was that like?

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: How often do you meet?

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: What's the discussion?

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: I'll try and explain that.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: So sometime in early 1989, two people, one from IBM, one from HP turned up in my office

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: and told me I would like to standardize C plus plus.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: This was a new idea to me.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: And I pointed out that it wasn't finished yet and it wasn't ready for formal

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: standardization and such.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: And they say, no, Bjarne, you haven't gotten it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: You really want to do this.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: Our organizations depend on C plus plus.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: We cannot depend on something that's owned by another corporation that might be a

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: competitor.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: Of course we could rely on you, but you might get run over by a bus.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: Right.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: The old bus.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: We really need to get this out in the open.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: It has to be standardized under formal rules.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: And we are going to standardize it under ISO rules.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: And you really want to be part of it because basically otherwise we'll do it ourselves.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: And we know you can do it better.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: So through a combination of arm twisting and flattery, it carries on.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: It got started.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: So in late 89, there was a meeting in DC at the, actually, no, it was not ISO then.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: It was ANSI, the American national standard we're doing.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: We met there.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: We were lectured on the rules of how to do an ANSI standard.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: There was about 25 of us there, which apparently was a new record for that kind

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: of meeting.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: And some of the old C guys that has been standardized in C was there.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: So we got some expertise in.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: So the way this works is that it's an open process.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: Anybody can sign up if they pay the minimal fee, which is about a thousand dollars.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: There's less than, it's a little bit more now.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: And I think it's $1,280.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: It's not going to kill you.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: And we have three meetings a year.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: This is fairly standard.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: We tried two meetings a year for a couple of years that didn't work too well.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: So three, one week meetings a year.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: And you meet and you have technical discussions and then you bring proposals

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: forward for votes.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: The votes are done one person per one vote per organization.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: So you can't have say IBM come in with 10 people and dominate things.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: That's not allowed.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: And these are organizations that extends to the UC plus plus.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: Yes.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: Because it's basically all individuals or individuals.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: I mean, it's a bunch of people in the room deciding the design of a language based on

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: which a lot of the world's systems run.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: That's right.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: Well, I think most people would agree it's better than if I decided it or better than

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: if a single organization like H&T decided it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: I don't know if everyone agrees to that, by the way, bureaucracies have their critics

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: too.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: Yes, they, they're there.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: Look, standardization is not pleasant.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: It's, it's, it's, it's, it's horrifying.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: It's like democracy.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: But we exactly, as Churchill says, democracy is the worst way except for the others.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: Right.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: And it's, I would say the same with formal standardization, but anyway, so we meet and

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: we, we, we have these votes and that determines what the standard is.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: Couple of years later, we extended this.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: So it became worldwide.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: We have standard organizations that are active in currently 15 to 20 countries and another

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: 15 to 20 are sort of looking and voting based on the rest of the work on it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: And we meet three times a year.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: Next week I'll be in Cologne, Germany, spending a week doing standardization and we'll vote

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: out the committee draft or C++ 20, which goes to the national standards committees for

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: comments and requests for changes and improvements.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: Then we do that.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: And there's a second set of votes where hopefully everybody votes in favor.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: This has happened several times.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: The first time we finished, we started in the first technical meeting was in 1990.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: The last was in 98.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: We voted it out.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: That was the standard that people used till 11 or a little bit past 11.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: Um, and it was an international standard.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: All the countries voted in favor.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: Um, it took long to get to the national standards.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: And it took longer with 11.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: I'll mention why, but all the nations voted in favor.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: And we work on the basis of a consensus.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: That is, we do not want something that passes 60 40, uh, because then we're getting,

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: getting a dialettes and opponents and people complain too much.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: They all complain too much, but basically it has no real effect.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: The, the standards has been obeyed.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: They have been working to make it, uh, easier to use many compilers,

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: many computers and all of that kind of stuff.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: And so the first, the, the, it was traditional with ISO standards to take 10 years.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: We did the first one and eight brilliant.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: And we thought we were going to do the next one and six because now we are good at it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: Right.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: It took 13.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: Yeah.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: It was named O X.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: It was named O X.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: Hoping that you would at least get it within the single, within the odds, the single digit.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: I thought we would get, I thought would get six, seven or eight.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: The confidence of youth.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: Yeah, that's right.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: Well, the point is that this was sort of like a second, um, system effect.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: That is we now knew how to do it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: And so we're going to do it much better and we've got more ambitious and it took longer.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: Furthermore, there is this tendency because it's a 10 year cycle or eight doesn't matter.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: Just before you're about to ship, somebody has a bright idea.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: Yeah.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: And so we really, really must get that in.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: We, we did that successfully with the STL.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: We got the standard library that gives us all the STL stuff that, that I basically,

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: I think it saved C plus plus.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: It was beautiful.

body.input: The way a constructor can establish the environment for the use of the, of a type for an object.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: That is key to C plus plus. That's why we don't have to use garbage collection.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: That's how we can get predictable performance.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: That's how you can get the minimal overhead in many, many cases and have really clean types.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: It's the idea of construct the destructor pairs.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: Sometimes it comes out under the name R I R I R I R I.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

body.input: It's also the best example of why I shouldn't be in advertising.

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48

metadata.title: Podcast: Bjarne Stroustrup: C++ | Lex Fridman Podcast #48
