metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: I'm trying to visualize what dynamic inference would be in this case. What is it doing with the

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: input? It's showing the input the first time. What's changing over temporally? What's the

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: dynamics of this inference process? So, you can think of it as you have,

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: at the top of the model, the characters that you are trained on. They are the causes. You're trying

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: to explain the pixels using the characters as the causes. The characters are the things that cause

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: the pixels. Yeah. So, there's this causality thing. So, the reason you mentioned causality,

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: I guess, is because there's a temporal aspect to this whole thing.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: In this particular case, the temporal aspect is not important. It is more like

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: when if I turn the character on, the pixels will turn on. Yeah. It will be after there's a little

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: bit, but yeah. So, it's causality in the sense of like a logic causality, like hence inference.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: Okay. The dynamics is that even though locally it will look like, okay, this is an A.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: And locally, when I look at just that patch of the image, it looks like an A. But when I look at it

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: in the context of all the other causes, it might not, A is not something that makes sense. So,

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: that is something you have to kind of recursively figure out. Yeah. So, okay. And this thing

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: performed pretty well on the captures. Correct. And I mean, is there some kind of interesting

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: intuition you can provide? Why it did well? What did it look like? Is there visualizations that

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: could be human interpretable to us humans? Yes. Yeah. So, the good thing about the model is that

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: it is extremely... So, it is not just doing a classification. It is providing a full explanation

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: for the scene. So, when it operates on a scene, it is coming back and saying, look, this is the part

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: is the A, and these are the pixels that turned on. These are the pixels in the input that makes me

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: think that it is an A. And also, these are the portions I hallucinated. It provides a complete

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: explanation of that form. And then, these are the contours. This is the interior, and this is in

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: front of this other object. So, that's the kind of explanation the inference network provides.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: So, that is useful and interpretable. And then, the kind of errors it makes are also...

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: I don't want to read too much into it, but the kind of errors the network makes are very similar

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: to the kinds of errors humans would make in a similar situation. So, there's something about

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: the structure that feels reminiscent of the way humans visual system works. Well, I mean,

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: how hard-coded is this to the capture problem, this idea? Not really hard-coded because it's the

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: assumptions, as I mentioned, are general, right? And those themselves can be applied in many

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: situations which are natural signals. So, it's the foreground versus background factorization,

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: and the factorization of the surfaces versus the contours. So, these are all generally applicable

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: assumptions. In all vision. So, why attack the capture problem, which is quite interesting.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: Why attack the capture problem, which is quite unique in the computer vision context versus

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: the traditional benchmarks of ImageNet and all those kinds of image classification, or even

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: segmentation tasks and all that kind of stuff. Do you feel like that's... I mean, what's your

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: thinking about those kinds of benchmarks in this context? I mean, those benchmarks are useful for

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: algorithms where you... So, the settings that deep learning works in are, here is my huge training

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: set, and here is my test set. So, the training set is almost 100x, 1000x bigger than the test set in

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: many cases. What we wanted to do was invert that. The training set is way smaller than the test set.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: Yes. And capture is a problem that is by definition hard for computers, and it has these

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: good properties of strong generalization, strong out of training distribution generalization. If

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: you are interested in studying that and having your model have that property, then it's a good

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: data set to tackle. So, have you attempted to, which I think I believe there's quite a growing

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: body of work on looking at MNIST and ImageNet without training? So, taking... The basic challenge

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: is what tiny fraction of the training set can we take in order to do a reasonable job of the

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: classification task? Have you explored that angle in these classic benchmarks?

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: Yes. So, we did do MNIST. So, it's not just capture. So, there was also

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: multiple versions of MNIST, including the standard version, where we inverted the problem,

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: which is basically saying rather than train on 60,000 training data, how quickly can you get

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: to high level accuracy with very little training data?

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: Is there some performance that you remember? How well did it do? How many examples did it need?

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: Yeah. I remember that it was on the order of

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: tens or hundreds of examples to get into 95% accuracy, and it was definitely better than

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: the other systems out there at that time. At that time. Yeah. Yeah. They're really

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: pushing it. I think that's a really interesting space, actually. I think there's an actual name

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: for MNIST that... There's different names to the different sizes of training sets. I mean,

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: people are attacking this problem. I think it's super interesting. It's funny how the MNIST will

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: probably be with us all the way to AGI as a data set that just sticks by. It's a clean, simple

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: data set to study the fundamentals of learning with. Just like CAPTCHAs, it's interesting.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: Correct. Not enough people... I don't know, maybe you can correct me, but I feel like CAPTCHAs don't

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: show up as often in papers as they probably should. That's correct. Yeah. Because usually these

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: things have a momentum. Once something gets established as a standard benchmark, there is

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: a dynamics of how graduate students operate and how the academic system works that pushes people

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: to track that benchmark. Nobody wants to think outside the box. Okay. Good performance on the

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: CAPTCHAs. What else is there interesting on the RCN side before we talk about the cortical

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: microswitch? Yeah. The same model. The important part of the model was that it trains very quickly

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: with very little training data. It's quite robust to out of distribution perturbations.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: We are using that very fruitfully in... Advocatious in many of the robotic tasks we are solving.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: Let me ask you this touchy question. I have spoken with your friend, colleague, Jeff Hawkins,

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: too. I have to ask, whenever you have brain-inspired stuff and you make big claims,

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: big sexy claims, there's critics, machine learning subreddit. Don't give me that name.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: Machine learning subreddit. Don't give me started on those people. Criticism is good, but they're

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: a bit over the top. There is quite a bit of skepticism and criticism. Is this work

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: really as good as it promises to be? Do you have thoughts on that kind of skepticism?

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: Do you have comments on the kind of criticism we might have received about, is this approach

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: legit? Is this a promising approach? Or at least as promising as it seems to be advertised as?

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: Yeah, I can comment on it. Our Arsene paper is published in Science, which I would argue is a

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: very high quality journal, very hard to publish in. Usually it is indicative of the quality of the

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: work. I am very, very certain that the ideas that we brought together in that paper, in terms of

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: the importance of feedback connections, recursive inference, lateral connections,

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: coming to best explanation of the scene as the problem to solve, trying to solve recognition,

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: segmentation, all jointly in a way that is compatible with higher level cognition, top-down

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: attention, all those ideas that we brought together into something coherent and workable

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: in the world and tackling a challenging problem. I think that will stay and that contribution I

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: stand by. Now, I can tell you a story which is funny in the context of this. If you read the

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: abstract of the paper and the argument we are putting in, look, current deep learning systems

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: take a lot of training data. They don't use these insights. Here is our new model, which is not a

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: deep neural network. It's a graphical model. It does inference. This is how the paper is.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: Once the paper was accepted and everything, it went to the press department in science,

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: AAAS, science office. We didn't do any press release when it was published. It went to the

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: press department. What was the press release that they wrote up? A new deep learning model.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: Solves captures. Solves captures. You can see what was being hyped in that thing.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: There is a dynamic in the community. That especially happens when there are lots of new

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: people coming into the field and they get attracted to one thing. Some people are trying to think

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: different compared to that. I think skepticism is important in science and it is very much

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: required. But it's also not skepticism. Usually, it's mostly bandwagon effect that is happening.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: But that's not even that. I'll tell you what they react to, which I'm sensitive to as well.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: If you look at just companies, OpenAI, DeepMind, Vicarious, there's a little bit of a race

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: to the top and hype. It doesn't pay off to be humble.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: And the press is just irresponsible often. Don't get me started on the state of journalism today.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: It seems like the people who write articles about these things, they literally have not even spent

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: an hour on the Wikipedia article about what is neural networks. They haven't invested just even

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: the language to laziness. It's like robots beat humans. They write this kind of stuff.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: The researchers are quite sensitive to that because it gets a lot of attention. They're like,

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: why did this work get so much attention? That's over the top and people get really sensitive.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: The same kind of criticism with OpenAI did work with Rubik's Cube, with the robot that people

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: criticized. Same with GPT-2 and 3. They criticized the same thing with DeepMinds, with AlphaZero.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: I'm sensitive to it. And of course, with your work, you mentioned deep learning, but there's

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: something super sexy to the public about brain inspired. That immediately grabs people's

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: imagination. Not even neural networks, but really brain inspired, brain like neural networks.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: That seems really compelling to people and to me as well, to the world as a narrative.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: People hook onto that and sometimes the skepticism engine turns on in the research community and

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: they're skeptical. But I think putting aside the ideas of the actual performance on CAPTCHAs or

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: performance on any data set, to me, all these data sets are useless anyway. It's nice to have them,

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: but in the grand scheme of things, they're silly toy examples. The point is, is there intuition

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: about the ideas, just like you mentioned, bringing the ideas together in a unique way?

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: Is there something there? Is there some value there? And is it going to stand the test of time?

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: My confidence there is very high. I don't treat brain inspired as a marketing term.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: I am looking into the details of biology and puzzling over those things and I am grappling

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: with those things. It is not a marketing term at all. You can use it as a marketing term and

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: people often use it and you can get combined with them. When people don't understand how we're

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: approaching the problem, it is easy to be misunderstood and think of it as purely marketing.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: But that's not the way we are. As a scientist, you believe that if we just stick to really

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: understanding the brain, you should constantly meditate on how does the brain do this?

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: Because that's going to be really helpful for engineering intelligent systems.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: I think it's one input and it is helpful, but you should know when to deviate from it too.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: An example is convolutional neural networks. Convolution is not an operation brain

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: implements. The visual cortex is not convolutional. The visual cortex has local receptive fields,

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: local connectivity, but there is no translation invariance in the network weights in the visual

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: cortex. That is a computational trick, which is a very good engineering trick that we use

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: for sharing the training between the different nodes. That trick will be with us for some time.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: It will go away when we have robots with eyes and heads that move. Then that trick will go away.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: It will not be useful at that time. The brain doesn't have translational

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: invariance. It has a focal point. It has a thing it focuses on. It has a fovea. Because of the fovea,

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: the receptive fields are not like the copying of the weights. The weights in the center are

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: very different from the weights in the periphery. I did this. I actually wrote a paper and just

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: got an chance to really study peripheral vision, which is a fascinating thing. Very

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: under-understood thing of what the brain does at every level with the periphery. It does some funky

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: stuff. It's another kind of trick than convolutional. Convolution in neural networks is a trick for

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: efficiency. The brain does a whole other kind of thing, I guess.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: You need to understand the principles or processing so that you can still apply engineering tricks

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: where you want to do. You don't want to be slavishly mimicking all the things of the brain.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: It should be one input. I think it is extremely helpful. It should be the point of really

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: understanding so that you know when to deviate from it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: Okay. That's really cool. That's work from a few years ago. You did work in Umenta with Jeff

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: Hawkins with hierarchical temporal memory. If you could give a brief history, how has your view

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: of the way the models of the brain changed over the past few years leading up to now?

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: Is there some interesting aspects where there was an adjustment to your understanding of the brain,

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: or is it all just building on top of each other? In terms of the higher level ideas,

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: especially the ones Jeff wrote about in the book, if you blur out the details and if you just zoom

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: out and at the higher level idea, things are, I would say, consistent with what he wrote about.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: But many things will be consistent with that because deep learning systems are also multi-level,

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: hierarchical, all of those things. But in terms of the detail, a lot of things are different,

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: and those details matter a lot. One point of difference I had with Jeff

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: was how much of biological plausibility and realism do you want in the learning algorithms?

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: So when I was there, this was almost 10 years ago now.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: That flies when you're having fun.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: I don't know what Jeff thinks now, but 10 years ago, the difference was that I did not want to

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: be so constrained on saying my learning algorithms need to be biologically plausible

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: based on some filter of biological plausibility available at that time. To me, that is a

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: dangerous cut to make because we are discovering more and more things about the brain all the time.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: New biophysical mechanisms, new channels are being discovered all the time. So I don't want to

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: up front kill off a learning algorithm just because we don't really understand the full

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: biophysics of how the brain learns.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: Exactly.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: Let me ask Sergeant Chaurabh, what's your sense? What's our best understanding of how the brain

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: learns?

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: Things like back propagation, credit assignment. Many of these learning algorithms have things in

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: common. Back propagation is one way of credit assignment. There is another algorithm called

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: expectation maximization, which is another weight adjustment algorithm.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: But is your sense the brain does something like this?

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: Has to. There is no way around it in the sense of saying that you do have to adjust the connections.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: So you're saying credit assignment, you have to reward the connections that were useful in

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: making a correct prediction. I guess it doesn't have to be differentiable.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: Yeah, it doesn't have to be differentiable. But you have a model that you start with,

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: you have data comes in, and you have to have a way of adjusting the model such that it better

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: fits the data. So that is all of learning. And some of them can be using backprop to do that.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: Some of it can be using very local graph changes to do that. Many of these learning algorithms have

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: similar update properties locally in terms of what the neurons need to do locally.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: I wonder if small differences in learning algorithms can have huge differences in the

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: actual effect. So the dynamics of sort of the reverse spiking, if credit assignment is like

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: a lightning versus a rainstorm or something, whether there's a looping local type of situation

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: with the credit assignment, whether there is regularization, how it injects robustness into

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: the whole thing, whether it's chemical or electrical or mechanical, all those kinds of things.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: I feel like those differences could be essential, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: It could be. It's just that you don't know enough to, on the learning side,

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: you don't know enough to say that is definitely not the way the brain does it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: Got it. So you don't want to be stuck to it. So you've been open-minded on that side of things.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: Correct. On the inference side, on the recognition side, I am much more amenable to being constrained

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: because it's much easier to do experiments because it's like, okay, here's the stimulus.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: How many steps did it get to take the answer? I can trace it back. I can understand the speed

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: of that computation, et cetera, much more readily on the inference side.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: Got it. And then you can't do good experiments on the learning side.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: Correct.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: So let's go right into the cortical microcircuits right back. So what are these ideas beyond

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: recursive cortical network that you're looking at now?

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: So we have made a pass through multiple of the steps that, as I mentioned earlier,

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: we were looking at perception from the angle of cognition. It was not just perception for

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: perception sake. How do you connect it to cognition? How do you learn concepts? And

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: how do you learn abstract reasoning similar to some of the things Francois talked about?

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: So we have taken one pass through it, basically saying, what is the basic cognitive architecture

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: that you need to have, which has a perceptual system, which has a system that learns dynamics

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: of the world, and then has something like a routine program learning system on top of it

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: to learn concepts. So we have built the version point one of that system,

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: this was another science robotics paper. The title of that paper was something like cognitive

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: programs. How do you build cognitive programs? And the application there was on manipulation,

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: robotic manipulation?

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: It was, so think of it like this. Suppose you wanted to tell a new person that you met,

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: you don't know the language that person uses, you want to communicate to that person to achieve

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: some task. So I want to say, hey, you need to pick up all the red cups from the kitchen counter

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: and put it here. How do you communicate that? You can show pictures, you can basically say,

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: look, this is the starting state, the things are here, this is the ending state, how do you

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: communicate that? And what does the person need to understand from that? The person needs to

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: understand what conceptually happened in those pictures from the input to the output. So we are

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: looking at pre-verbal conceptual understanding. Without language, how do you have a set of

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: concepts that you can manipulate in your head? And from a set of images of input and output,

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: can you infer what is happening in those images?

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: Got it. With concepts that are pre-language, okay. So what does it mean for a concept to be pre-language?

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: Yeah.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: Why is language so important here?

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: So I want to make a distinction between concepts that are just learned from text by just feeding

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: brute force text. You can start extracting things like, okay, cow is likely to be on grass.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: So those kinds of things you can extract purely from text. But that's kind of a simple association

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: thing rather than a concept as an abstraction of something that happens in the real world

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: in a grounded way that I can simulate it in my mind and then I can use it to make

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: it in my mind and connect it back to the real world.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: And you think kind of the visual world, concepts in the visual world are somehow lower level

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: than just the language?

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: The lower level kind of makes it feel like, okay, that's like an unimportant, like it's

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: more like I would say the concepts in the visual and the motor system and the concept

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: learning system, which if you cut off the language part, just what we learn by interacting

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: with the world and abstractions from that, that is a prerequisite for any real language

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: understanding.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: So you disagree with Chomsky because he says language is at the bottom of everything.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: No, I disagree with Chomsky completely on how many levels from universal grammar to

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: yeah.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: So that was a paper in science beyond the recursive cortical network. What other interesting

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: problems are there, the open problems and brain inspired approaches that you're thinking

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: about?

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: I mean, everything is open, right? Like no problem is solved, solved. I think of perception

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: as kind of the first thing that you have to build, but the last thing that you will be

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: actually solved. Because if you do not build perception system in the right way, you cannot

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: build concept system in the right way. So you have to build a perception system, however

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: wrong that might be, you have to still build that and learn concepts from there and then

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: keep iterating. And finally, perception will get solved fully when perception, cognition,

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: language, all those things work together finally.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: So great, we've talked a lot about perception, but then maybe on the concept side and like

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: common sense or just general reasoning side, is there some intuition you can draw from

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: the brain about how we could do that?

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: So I have this classic example I give. So suppose I give you a few sentences and then

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: ask you a question following that sentence. This is a natural language processing problem,

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: right? So here it goes. I'm telling you, Sally pounded a nail on the ceiling. Okay, that's

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: a sentence. Now I'm asking you a question, was the nail horizontal or vertical?

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: Vertical.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: Okay, how did you answer that?

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: Well, I imagined Sally, it was kind of hard to imagine what the hell she was doing, but

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: I imagined a visual of the whole situation.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: Exactly, exactly. So here, I post a question in natural language. The answer to that question

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: was you got the answer from actually simulating the scene. Now I can go more and more detail

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: about, okay, was Sally standing on something while doing this? Could she have been standing

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: on a light bulb to do this? I could ask more and more questions about this and I can ask,

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: make you simulate the scene in more and more detail, right? Where is all that knowledge

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: that you're accessing stored? It is not in your language system. It was not just by reading

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: text you got that knowledge. It is stored from the everyday experiences that you have

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: had. By the age of five, you have pretty much all of this, right? It is stored in your visual

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: system, motor system, in a way such that it can be accessed through language.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: Got it. I mean, right. So the language is just almost sort of the query into the whole

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: visual cortex and that does the whole feedback thing. But I mean, it is all reasoning kind

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: of connected to the perception system in some way.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: You can do a lot of it. You can still do a lot of it by quick associations without having

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: to go into the depth. And most of the time you will be right, right? You can just do

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: quick associations, but I can easily create tricky situations for you where that quick

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: association is wrong and you have to actually run the simulation.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: So figuring out how these concepts connect, do you have a good idea of how to do that?

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: That's exactly what one of the problems that we are working on. And the way we are approaching

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: that is basically saying, okay, you need to... So the takeaway is that language is simulation

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: control and your perceptual plus motor system is building a simulation of the world. And

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: so that's basically the way we are approaching it. And the first thing that we built was

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: a controllable perceptual system and we built a schema networks, which was a controllable

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: dynamic system. Then we built a concept learning system that puts all these things together

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: into programs or subtractions that you can run and simulate. And now we are taking the

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: step of connecting it to language. And it will be very simple examples initially. It

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: will not be the GPT-3 like examples, but it will be grounded simulation-based language.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: And for like the querying would be like question answering kind of thing?

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: Correct. And it will be in some simple world initially, but it will be about, okay, can

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: the system connect the language and grounded in the right way and run the right simulations

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: to come up with the answer.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: And the goal is to try to do things that, for example, GPT-3 couldn't do.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: Correct.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: Speaking of which, if we could talk about GPT-3 a little bit, I think it's an interesting

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: thought-provoking set of ideas that OpenAI is pushing forward. I think it's good for

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: us to talk about the limits and the possibilities in neural networks. So in general, what are

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: your thoughts about this recently released very large 175 billion parameter language

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: model?

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: So I haven't directly evaluated it yet. From what I have seen on Twitter and other people

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: evaluating it, it looks very intriguing. I am very intrigued by some of the properties

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: it is displaying. And of course, the text generation part of that was already evident

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: in GPT-2, that it can generate coherent text over long distances. But of course, the weaknesses

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: are also pretty visible in saying that, okay, it is not really carrying a world state around.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: And sometimes you get sentences like, I went up the hill to reach the valley or something

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: like that, some completely incompatible statements. Or when you're traveling from one place to

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: the other, it doesn't take into account the time of travel, things like that. So those

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: things I think will happen less in GPT-3 because it is trained on even more data and it can

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: do even more longer distance coherence. But it will still have the fundamental limitations

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

body.input: that it doesn't have a world model and it can't run simulations in its head to find

metadata.title: Podcast: Dileep George: Brain-Inspired AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #115

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: On the other hand, it is your escape.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: And everyone has these things that are very personal to them.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: So what we've found is that when it comes to...

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: Most people claim that they have a friend or two that they are heavily inspired by and that they listen to.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: So I actually think music is very social, but in a smaller group setting, it's an intimate form of...

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: It's an intimate relationship.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: It's not something that you necessarily share broadly.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: Now, at concerts, you can argue you do, but then you've gathered a lot of people that you have something in common with.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: I think this broadcast sharing of music is something we tried on social networks and so forth.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: But it turns out that people aren't super interested in what their friends listen to.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: They're interested in understanding if they have something in common, perhaps, with a friend, but not just as information.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: Right. That's really interesting.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: I was just thinking this morning, listening to Spotify.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: I really have a pretty intimate relationship with Spotify, with my playlists.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: I've had them for many years now, and they've grown with me together.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: There's an intimate relationship you have with a library of music that you've developed.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: And we'll talk about different ways we can play with that.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: Can you do the impossible task and try to give a history of music listening from your perspective, from before the Internet and after the Internet?

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: And just kind of everything leading up to streaming Spotify and so on?

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: I'll try. It could be a 100-year podcast.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: I'll try to do a brief version.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: There are some things that I think are very interesting during the history of music, which is that,

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: before recording music, to be able to enjoy music, you actually had to be where the music was produced,

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: because you couldn't record it and time shift it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: Creation and consumption had to happen at the same time.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: Basically, concerts. And so you either had to get to the nearest village to listen to music.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: And while that was cumbersome and it severely limited the distribution of music,

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: it also had some different qualities, which was that the creator could always interact with the audience.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: It was always live. And also, there was no time cap on the music.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: So I think it's not a coincidence that these early classical works, they're much longer than the three minutes.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: The three minutes came in as a restriction of the first wax disc that could only contain

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: a three-minute song on one side.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: So actually, the recorded music severely limited the...

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: Or put constraints. I won't say limit. I mean, constraints are often good,

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: but it put very hard constraints on the music format.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: So you kind of said, instead of doing this opus on like many tens of minutes or something,

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: now you get three and a half minutes because then you're out of wax on this disc.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: But in return, you get an amazing distribution. Your reach will widen.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: Just on that point real quick, without the mass scale distribution, there's a scarcity component

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: where you kind of look forward to it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: We had that... It's like the Netflix versus HBO Game of Thrones.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: You wait for the event because you can't really listen to it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: So you look forward to it and then you derive perhaps more pleasure because it's more rare

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: for you to listen to a particular piece.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: Do you think there's value to that scarcity?

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: Yeah, I think that is definitely a thing.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: And there's always this component of if you have something in infinite amounts,

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: will you value it as much?

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: Probably not.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: Humanity is always seeking some... Is relative.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: So you're always seeking something you didn't have and when you have it,

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: you don't appreciate it as much.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: So I think that's probably true. But I think that's why concerts exist.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: So you can actually have both.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: But I think net, if you couldn't listen to music in your car driving, that'd be worse.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: That cost would be bigger than the benefit of the anticipation I think that you would have.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: So, yeah, it started with live concerts, then being able to...

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: The phonograph invented, right? You started to be able to record music.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: Exactly. So then you got this massive distribution that made it possible to create two things,

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: I think. First of all, cultural phenomenons.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: They probably need distribution to be able to happen.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: But it also opened access for a new kind of artist.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: So you started to have these phenomenons like Beatles and Elvis and so forth.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: That was really a function of distribution, I think, obviously, of talent and innovation.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: But there was also a technical component.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: And of course, the next big innovation to come along was radio, broadcast radio.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: And I think radio is interesting because it started not as a music medium,

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: it started as an information medium for news.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: And then radio needed to find something to fill the time with so that they could honestly

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: play more ads and make more money. And music was free.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: So then you had this massive distribution where you could program to people.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: I think those things, that ecosystem is what created the ability for hits.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: But it was also a very broadcast medium.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: So you would tend to get these massive, massive hits, but maybe not such a long tail.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: In terms of choice, of everybody listening to the same stuff.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: Yeah. And as you said, I think there are some social benefits to that.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: I think, for example, there's a high statistical chance that if I talk about the latest episode

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: of Game of Thrones, we have something to talk about just statistically.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: In the age of individual choice, maybe some of that goes away.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: So I do see the value of shared cultural components, but I also obviously love personalization.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: And so let's catch this up to the Internet.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: So maybe Napster.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: Well, first of all, there's like MP3s.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: Exactly. There's like tapes, CDs.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: There was a digitalization of music with a CD, really.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: It was physical distribution, but the music became digital.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: And so they were files, but basically boxed software to use a software analogy.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: And then you could start downloading these files.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: And I think there are two interesting things that happened.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: Back to music used to be longer before it was constrained by the distribution medium.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: I don't think that was a coincidence.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: And then really the only music genre to have developed mostly after

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: music was a file again on the Internet is EDM.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: And EDM is often much longer than the traditional music.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: I think it's interesting to think about the fact that music is no longer constrained in

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: minutes per song or something.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: It's a legacy of an old distribution technology.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: And you see some of this new music that breaks the format.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: Not so much as I would have expected, actually, by now, but it still happens.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: So first of all, I don't really know what EDM is.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: Electronic dance music.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: You could say Avicii was one of the biggest in this genre.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: So the main constraint is of time, something that three, four, five minutes song.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: So you could have songs that were eight minutes, 10 minutes and so forth.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: Because it started as a digital product that you downloaded.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: So you didn't have this constraint anymore.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: So I think it's something really interesting that I don't think has fully happened yet.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: We're kind of jumping ahead a little bit to where we are.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: But I think there's tons of form and innovation in music that should happen now.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: That couldn't happen when you needed to really adhere to the distribution constraints.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: If you didn't adhere to that, you would get no distribution.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: So Björk, for example, Icelandic artist, she made a full iPad app as an album.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: That's very expensive.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: Even though the app store has great distribution, she gets nowhere near the distribution versus staying within the three minute format.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: So I think now that music is fully digital inside these streaming services, there is the opportunity to change the format again.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: And allow creators to be much more creative without limiting their distribution ability.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: That's interesting that you're right.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: It's surprising that we don't see that taken advantage more often.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: It's almost like the constraints of the distribution from the 50s and 60s have molded the culture to where we want the three to five minute song.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: That anything else, not just so we want the song as consumers and as artists.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: Because I write a lot of music and I never even thought about writing something longer than 10 minutes.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: It's really interesting that those constraints.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: Because all your training data has been three and a half minute songs.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: That's right.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: So yeah, digitization of data led to then MP3s.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: Yeah, so I think you had this file then that was distributed physically.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: But then you had the components of digital distribution and then the internet happened.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: And there was this vacuum where you had a format that could be digitally shipped, but there was no business model.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: And then all these pirate networks happened.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: Napster and in Sweden, Pirate Bay, which was one of the biggest.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: I think from a consumer point of view, which kind of leads up to the inception of Spotify.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: From a consumer point of view, consumers for the first time had this access model to music.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: Where they could, without any marginal cost, they could try different tracks.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: You could use music in new ways. There was no marginal cost.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: And that was a fantastic consumer experience to have access to all the music ever made.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: I think was fantastic.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: But it was also horrible for artists because there was no business model around it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: So they didn't make any money.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: So the user need almost drove the user interface before there was a business model.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: And then there were these download stores that allowed you to download files, which was a solution.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: But it didn't solve the access problem.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: There was still a marginal cost of 99 cents to try one more track.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: And I think that heavily limits how you listen to music.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: The example I always give is in Spotify, a huge amount of people listen to music while they sleep.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: While they go to sleep and while they sleep.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: If that costed you 99 cents per three minutes, you probably wouldn't do that.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: And you would be much less adventurous if there was a real dollar cost to exploring music.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: So the access model is interesting in that it changes your music behavior.
