metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: You can take much more risk because there's no marginal cost to it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: Maybe let me linger on piracy for a second.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: I find, especially coming from Russia, piracy is something that's very interesting.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: For me, not me of course ever, but I have friends who have partook in piracy of music, software, TV shows, sporting events.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: And usually to me what that shows is not that they can actually pay the money and they're not trying to save money.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: They're choosing the best experience.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: So what to me piracy shows is a business opportunity in all these domains.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: And that's where I think you're right.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: Spotify stepped in is basically piracy is an experience you can explore with fine music you like.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: And actually the interface of piracy is horrible because it's...

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: Bad metadata.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: Yeah, bad metadata.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: Long download times, all kinds of stuff.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: And what Spotify does is basically first rewards artists and second makes the experience of exploring music much better.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: The same is true I think for movies and so on.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: Piracy reveals in the software space, for example, I'm a huge user and fan of Adobe products.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: And there was much more incentive to pirate Adobe products before they went to a monthly subscription plan.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: And now all of the said friends that used to pirate Adobe products that I know now actually pay gladly for the monthly subscription.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: Yeah, I think you're right.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: I think it's a sign of an opportunity for product development and that sometimes there's a product market fit before there's a business model fit in product development.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: I think that's a sign of it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: In Sweden, I think it was a bit of both.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: There was a culture where we even had a political party called the Pirate Party.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: And this was during the time when people said that information should be free.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: It was somehow wrong to charge for ones and zeros.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: So I think people felt that artists should probably make some money somehow else in concerts or something.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: So at least in Sweden, it was part really social acceptance even at the political level.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: But that also forced Spotify to compete with free, which I don't think would actually could have happened anywhere else in the world.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: The music industry needed to be doing bad enough to take that risk.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: And Sweden was like the perfect testing ground.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: It had government funded high bandwidth, low latency broadband, which meant that the product would work.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: And it was also there was no music revenue anyway.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: So they were kind of like, I don't think this is going to work, but why not?

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: So this product is one that I don't think could have happened in America.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: The world's largest music market, for example.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: So how do you compete with free?

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: Because that's an interesting world of the Internet where most people don't like to pay for things.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: So Spotify steps in and tries to, yes, compete with free.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: How do you do it?

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: So I think two things.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: One is people are starting to pay for things on the Internet.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: I think one way to think about it was that advertising was the first business model because no one would put the credit card on the Internet.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: Transactional with Amazon was the second and maybe subscription is the third.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: And if you look offline, subscription is the biggest of those.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: So that may still happen.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: I think people are starting to pay.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: But definitely back then we needed to compete with free.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: And the first thing you need to do is obviously to lower the price to free.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: And then you need to be better somehow.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: And the way that Spotify was better was on the user experience, on the actual performance, the latency of, you know, even if you had high bandwidth broadband,

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: it would still take you 30 seconds to a minute to download one of these tracks.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: So the Spotify experience of starting within the perceptual limit of immediacy, about 250 milliseconds,

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: meant that the whole trick was it felt as if you had downloaded all the part that it was on your hard drive.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: It was that fast, even though it wasn't.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: And it was still free.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: But somehow you were actually still being a legal citizen.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: That was the trick that Spotify managed to pull off.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: So I've actually heard you say this or write this.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: And I was surprised that I wasn't aware of it because I just took it for granted.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: You know, whenever an awesome thing comes along, you just like,

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: oh, of course it has to be this way.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: That's exactly right.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: That it felt like the entire world's libraries at my fingertips because of that latency being reduced.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: What was the technical challenge in reducing the latency?

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: So there was a group of really, really talented engineers, one of them called Ludwig Strigius.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: He wrote the, actually from Gothenburg, he wrote the initial, the U-Torrent client,

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: which is kind of an interesting backstory to Spotify, you know, that we have one of the top developers from,

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: from BitTorrent clients as well.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: So he wrote U-Torrent, the world's smallest BitTorrent client.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: And then he was acquired very early by Daniel and Martin, who founded Spotify.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: And they actually sold the U-Torrent client to BitTorrent, but kept Ludwig.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: So Spotify had a lot of experience within peer-to-peer networking.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: So the original innovation was a distribution innovation where Spotify built an end-to-end

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: media distribution system up until only a few years ago.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: We actually hosted all the music ourselves.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: So we had both the service side and the client.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: And that meant that we could do things such as having a peer-to-peer solution to use local caching

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: on the client side, because back then the world was mostly desktop.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: But we could also do things like hack the TCP protocols, things like Nagel's algorithm

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: for kind of exponential back-off or ramp up and just go full throttle and optimize for latency

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: at the cost of bandwidth.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: And all of this end-to-end control meant that we could do an experience that felt like a step change.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: These days, we actually are on GCP.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: We don't host our own stuff.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: And everyone is really fast these days.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: So that was the initial competitive advantage.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: But then obviously you have to move on over time.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: And that was, that was over 10 years ago, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: That was in 2008.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: The product was launched in Sweden.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: It was in a beta, I think 2007.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: And it was on the desktop, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: So it was desktop only.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: There's no phone.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: There was no phone.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: The iPhone came out in 2008, but the App Store came out one year later, I think.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: So the writing was on the wall, but there was no phone yet.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: You've mentioned that people would use Spotify to discover the songs they like,

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: and then they would torrent those songs so they can copy it to their phone.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: Just hilarious.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: Exactly.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: Oh, not torrent, pirate.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: Seriously, piracy does seem to be like a good guide for business models.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: Video content.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: As far as I know, Spotify doesn't have video content.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: Well, we do have music videos and we do have videos on the service.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: But the way we think about ourselves is that we're an audio service.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: And we think that if you look at the amount of time that people spend on audio,

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: it's actually very similar to the amount of time that people spend on video.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: So the opportunity should be equally big.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: But today it's not at all valued.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: Video is valued much higher.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: So we think it's basically completely undervalued.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: So we think of ourselves as an audio service.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: But within that audio service, I think video can make a lot of sense.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: I think when you're discovering an artist,

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: you probably do want to see them and understand who they are,

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: to understand their identity.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: You won't see that video every time.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: No, 90% of the time the phone is going to be in your pocket.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: For podcasters, you use video.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: I think that can make a ton of sense.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: So we do have video, but we're an audio service where,

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: think of it as we call it internally, backgroundable video.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: Video that is helpful, but isn't the driver of the narrative.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: I think also if you look at YouTube,

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: there's quite a few folks who listen to music on YouTube.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: So in some sense, YouTube is a bit of a competitor to Spotify,

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: which is very strange to me that people use YouTube to listen to music.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: They play essentially the music videos, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: But don't watch the videos and put it in their pocket.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: Well, I think it's similar to what, strangely,

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: maybe it's similar to what we were for the piracy networks,

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: where YouTube, for historical reasons, have a lot of music videos.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: So people use YouTube for a lot of the discovery part of the process, I think.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: But then it's not a really good sort of quote unquote MP3 player,

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: because it doesn't even background.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: Then you have to keep the app in the foreground.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: So it's not a good consumption tool, but it's a decently good discovery.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: I mean, I think YouTube is a fantastic product,

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: and I use it for all kinds of purposes, education and so forth.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: That's true. If I were to admit something,

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: I do use YouTube a little bit to assist in the discovery process of songs.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: And then if I like it, I'll add it to Spotify.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: But that's okay. That's okay with us.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: Okay, so sorry, we're jumping around a little bit.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: So this kind of incredible, you look at Napster,

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: you look at the early days of Spotify.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: One fascinating point is how do you grow a user base?

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: So you're there in Sweden, you have an idea.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: I saw the initial sketches that looked terrible.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: How do you grow a user base from a few folks to millions?

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: I think there are a bunch of tactical answers.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: So first of all, I think you need a great product.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: I don't think you take a bad product and market it to be successful.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: So you need a great product.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: But sorry to interrupt, but it's a totally new way to listen to music too.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: So it's not just, did people realize immediately that Spotify is a great product?

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: I think they did.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: So back to the point of piracy, it was a totally new way to listen to music legally.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: But people had been used to the access model in Sweden

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: and the rest of the world for a long time through piracy.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: So one way to think about Spotify, it was just legal and fast piracy.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: And so people have been using it for a long time.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: So they weren't alien to it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: They didn't really understand how it could be legal

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: because it seemed too fast and too good to be true,

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: which I think is a great product proposition if you can be too good to be true.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: But what I saw again and again was people showing each other,

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: clicking the song, showing how fast it started and saying,

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: can you believe this?

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: So I really think it was about speed.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: Then we also had an invite program that was really meant for scaling

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: because we hosted our own servers.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: We needed to control scaling, but that built a lot of expectation.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: And I don't want to say hype because hype implies that it wasn't true.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: Excitement.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: Excitement around the product.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: And we replicated that when we launched in the US.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: We also built up an invite only program first.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: There are lots of tactics,

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: but I think you need a great product that solves some problem.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: And basically, the key innovation, there was technology,

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: but on a meta level, the innovation was really the access model

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: versus the ownership model.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: And that was tricky.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: A lot of people said that they wanted to own their music.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: They would never kind of rent it or borrow it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: But I think the fact that we had a free tier,

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: which meant that you get to keep this music for life as well, helped quite a lot.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: So this is an interesting psychological point that maybe you can speak to.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: It was a big shift for me.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: It's almost like I had to go to therapy for this.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: I think I would describe my early listening experience,

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: and I think a lot of my friends do, as basically hoarding music.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: As you're slowly, one song by one song, or maybe albums,

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: gathering a collection of music that you love.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: And you own it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: Especially with CDs or tape, you physically had it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: And with Spotify, what I had to come to grips with,

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: and it was kind of liberating actually,

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: is to throw away all the music.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: I've had this therapy session with lots of people.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: And I think the mental trick is, so actually we've seen the user data.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: When Spotify started, a lot of people did the exact same thing.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: They started hoarding as if the music would disappear.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: Almost the equivalent of downloading.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: And so we had these playlists that had limits of a few hundred thousand tracks.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: And we figured no one will ever.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: Well, they do.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: It's in hundreds and hundreds of thousands of tracks.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: And to this day, some people want to actually save, quote unquote,

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: and apply the entire catalog.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: But I think the therapy session goes something like,

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: instead of throwing away your music,

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: if you took your files and you stored them in a locker at Google,

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: it'd be a streaming service.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: It's just that in that locker, you have all the world's music now for free.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: So instead of giving away your music, you got all the music.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: It's yours.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: You could think of it as having a copy of the world's catalog there forever.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: So you actually got more music instead of less.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: It's just that you just took that hard disk

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: and you sent it to someone who stored it for you.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: And once you go through that mental journey of like,

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: still my files, they're just over there,

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: and I just have 40 million or 50 million or something now,

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: then people are like, OK, that's good.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: The problem is, I think, because you paid us a subscription,

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: if we hadn't had the free tier, where you would feel like,

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: even if I don't want to pay anymore, I still get to keep them.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: You keep your playlist forever.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: They don't disappear even though you stop paying.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: I think that was really important.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: If we would have started as, you know, you can put in all this time,

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: but if you stop paying, you lose all your work.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: I think that would have been a big challenge

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: and was the big challenge for a lot of our competitors.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: That's another reason why I think the free tier is really important,

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: that people need to feel the security that the work they put in,

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: it will never disappear, even if they decide not to pay.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: I like how you put the work you put in.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: I actually stopped even thinking of it that way.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: Actually, Spotify taught me to just enjoy music,

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: as opposed to what I was doing before,

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: which is like in an unhealthy way hoarding music,

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: which I found that because I was doing that,

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: I was listening to a small selection of songs way too much,

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: to where I was getting sick of them.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: Whereas Spotify, the more liberating kind of approach,

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: is I was just enjoying, of course,

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: I listened to Stairway to Heaven over and over,

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: but because of the extra variety, I don't get as sick of them.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: There's an interesting statistic I saw.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: So Spotify has, maybe you can correct me,

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: but over 50 million songs, tracks, and over 3 billion playlists.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: So 50 million songs and 3 billion playlists.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: 60 times more playlists than songs.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: What do you make of that?

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: The way I think about it is that from a statistical machine learning point of view,

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: you have all these, if you want to think about reinforcement learning,

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: you have this state space of all the tracks,

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: and you can take different journeys through this world.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: I think of these as people helping themselves and each other,

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: creating interesting vectors through this space of tracks.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: And then it's not so surprising that across many tens of millions of atomic units,

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: there will be billions of paths that make sense.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: And we're probably pretty far away from having found all of them.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: So our job now is users, when Spotify started,

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: it was really a search box that was for the time pretty powerful.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: And then I like to refer to it as this programming language called playlisting,

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: where if you, as you probably were pretty good at music,

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: you knew your new releases, you knew your back catalog, you knew your start with the heaven,

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: you could create a soundtrack for yourself using this playlisting tool,

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: this like meta programming language for music, to soundtrack your life.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: And people who were good at music, it's back to how do you scale the product,

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: for people who were good at music, that wasn't actually enough.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: If you had the catalog in a good search tool, and you can create your own sessions,

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: you could create really good a soundtrack for your entire life.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: It's probably perfectly personalized because you did it yourself.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: But the problem was most people, many people aren't that good at music,

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: they just can't spend the time.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: Even if you're very good at music, it's going to be hard to keep up.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: So what we did to try to scale this was to essentially try to build,

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: you can think of them as agents, this friend that some people had

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: that helped them navigate this music catalog, that's what we're trying to do for you.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: But also there is something like 200 million active users on Spotify.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: So from the machine learning perspective, you have these 200 million people plus.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: They're creating, it's really interesting to think of a playlist as,

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: I don't know if you meant it that way, but it's almost like a programming language.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: It's at least a trace of exploration of those individual agents, the listeners.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: And you have all these new tracks coming in.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: So it's a fascinating space that is ripe for machine learning.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: So how can playlists be used as data in terms of machine learning

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: to help Spotify organize the music?

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: So we found in our data, not surprising, that people who playlisted a lot,

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: they retained much better, they had a great experience.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: And so our first attempt was to playlist for users.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: And so we acquired this company called Tunigo of editors and professional playlisters

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: and kind of leveraged the maximum of human intelligence

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: to help build these vectors through the track space for people.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: And that broadened the product.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: And we used statistical means where they could see when they created a playlist,

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: how did that playlist perform?

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: They could see skips of the songs, they could see how the songs perform,

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: and they manually iterated the playlist to maximize performance

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: for a large group of people.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: But there were never enough editors to playlist for you personally.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: So the promise of machine learning was to go from kind of group personalization

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: using editors and tools and statistics to individualization.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: And then what's so interesting about the 3 billion playlists we have is,

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: and the truth is we lucked out.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: This was not a priority strategy, as is often the case.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: It looks really smart in hindsight, but it was dumb luck.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: We looked at these playlists and we had some people in the company,

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: a person named Eric Bernodson,

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: who was really good at machine learning already back then in 2007, 2008.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: Back then it was mostly collaborative filtering and so forth.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: But we realized that what this is is people are grouping tracks for themselves

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: that have some semantic meaning to them.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: And then they actually label it with a playlist name as well.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: So in a sense, people were grouping tracks along semantic dimensions

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: and labeling them.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: And so could you use that information to find that latent embedding?

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: And so we started playing around with collaborative filtering

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: and we saw tremendous success with it,

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: basically trying to extract some of these dimensions.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: And if you think about it, it's not surprising at all.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: It would be quite surprising if playlists were actually random,

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: if they had no semantic meaning.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: For most people, they group these tracks for some reason.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: So we just happened to cross this incredible data set

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: where people had taken these tens of millions of tracks

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: and grouped them along different semantic vectors.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: And the semantics being outside the individual users,

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: so it's some kind of universal.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: There's a universal embedding that holds across people on this earth.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: Yes, I do think that the embeddings you find are going to be reflective

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: of the people who playlisted.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: So if you have a lot of indie lovers who playlist,

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: you're embedding is going to perform better there.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: But what we found was that, yes, there were these latent similarities.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: They were very powerful.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: And it was interesting because I think that the people who playlisted the most initially

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: were the so-called music aficionados who were really into music.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: And they often had a certain, their taste was often geared towards a certain type of music.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: And so what surprised us, if you look at the problem from the outside,

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: you might expect that the algorithms would start performing best with mainstreamers first

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: because it somehow feels like an easier problem to solve mainstream taste

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: than really particular taste.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: It was the complete opposite for us.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: The recommendations performed fantastically for people who saw themselves as having very unique taste.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: That's probably because all of them playlisted and they didn't perform so well for mainstreamers.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: They actually thought they were a bit too particular and unorthodox.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: So we had the complete opposite of what we expected,

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: success within the hardest problem first and then had to try to scale to more mainstream recommendations.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: So you've also acquired Echo Nest that analyzes song data.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: So in your view, maybe you can talk about what kind of data is there from a machine learning perspective.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: There's a huge amount, we're talking about play listing and just user data

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: of what people are listening to, the playlist they're constructing and so on.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: And then there's the actual data within a song, what makes a song, I don't know, the actual waveforms.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: How do you mix the two? How much value is there in each?

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: To me, it seems like user data is a romantic notion that the song itself would contain useful information.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: But if I were to guess, user data would be much more powerful.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: Like playlists would be much more powerful.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: Yeah, so we use both.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: Our biggest success initially was with playlist data

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: without understanding anything about the structure of the song.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: But when we acquired the Echo Nest, they had the inverse problem.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: They actually didn't have any play data.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: They were a provider of recommendations, but they didn't actually have any play data.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: So they looked at the structure of songs sonically,

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: and they looked at Wikipedia for cultural references and so forth, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: And did a lot of NLU and so forth.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: So we got that skill into the company and combined kind of our user data

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: with their kind of content-based.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: So you can think of it as we were user-based and they were content-based in their recommendations.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: And we combined those two.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: And for some cases where you have a new song that has no play data,

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: obviously you have to try to go by either who the artist is

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: or the sonic information in the song or what it's similar to.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: So there's definitely value in both, and we do a lot in both.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: But I would say yes, the user data captures things that have to do with culture

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: in the greater society that you would never see in the content itself.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: But that said, we have seen, we have a research lab in Paris.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: We can talk more about that kind of machine learning on the creator side,

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: what it can do for creators, not just for the consumers,

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: but where we looked at how does the structure of a song actually affect the listening behavior.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: And it turns out that there is a lot of, we can predict things like skips based on the song itself.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

body.input: We could say that maybe you should move that chorus a bit because your skip is going to go up here.

metadata.title: Podcast: Gustav Soderstrom: Spotify | Lex Fridman Podcast #29

metadata.title: Podcast: Georges St-Pierre, John Danaher & Gordon Ryan: The Greatest of All Time | Lex Fridman Podcast #260

body.input: hit and swarmed on. So there's a sense in which the biggest difference between them

metadata.title: Podcast: Georges St-Pierre, John Danaher & Gordon Ryan: The Greatest of All Time | Lex Fridman Podcast #260

body.input: is time of application of technique. In mixed martial arts, it's incredibly unforgiving

metadata.title: Podcast: Georges St-Pierre, John Danaher & Gordon Ryan: The Greatest of All Time | Lex Fridman Podcast #260

body.input: in terms of time. Even the smallest error can have the deepest consequences. In grappling,

metadata.title: Podcast: Georges St-Pierre, John Danaher & Gordon Ryan: The Greatest of All Time | Lex Fridman Podcast #260

body.input: you can make massive errors and still come back and win. Grappling will typically be

metadata.title: Podcast: Georges St-Pierre, John Danaher & Gordon Ryan: The Greatest of All Time | Lex Fridman Podcast #260

body.input: won in a much higher percentage case by the more skilled and conditioned grappler, whereas

metadata.title: Podcast: Georges St-Pierre, John Danaher & Gordon Ryan: The Greatest of All Time | Lex Fridman Podcast #260

body.input: there is much more of what they call a puncher's chance in mixed martial arts where there's

metadata.title: Podcast: Georges St-Pierre, John Danaher & Gordon Ryan: The Greatest of All Time | Lex Fridman Podcast #260

body.input: a much higher likelihood of a lesser athlete defeating a greater athlete in MMA than there

metadata.title: Podcast: Georges St-Pierre, John Danaher & Gordon Ryan: The Greatest of All Time | Lex Fridman Podcast #260

body.input: is in grappling simply because of time of application of the techniques. Even the smallest

metadata.title: Podcast: Georges St-Pierre, John Danaher & Gordon Ryan: The Greatest of All Time | Lex Fridman Podcast #260

body.input: period of inattention in MMA and the match is over. Gordon Ryan could fall asleep for

metadata.title: Podcast: Georges St-Pierre, John Danaher & Gordon Ryan: The Greatest of All Time | Lex Fridman Podcast #260

body.input: 30 seconds, have his opponent mounted on him, wake up and finish him five minutes later.

metadata.title: Podcast: Georges St-Pierre, John Danaher & Gordon Ryan: The Greatest of All Time | Lex Fridman Podcast #260

body.input: That's not going to happen in MMA.

metadata.title: Podcast: Georges St-Pierre, John Danaher & Gordon Ryan: The Greatest of All Time | Lex Fridman Podcast #260

body.input: Okay. So the stakes are much higher. You can do a lot of damage in a very small amount

metadata.title: Podcast: Georges St-Pierre, John Danaher & Gordon Ryan: The Greatest of All Time | Lex Fridman Podcast #260

body.input: of time and the just the dynamics, the temporal dynamics of how things happen is very different.

metadata.title: Podcast: Georges St-Pierre, John Danaher & Gordon Ryan: The Greatest of All Time | Lex Fridman Podcast #260

body.input: Everything you'll see will be a reflection of that. Then you go further into things like

metadata.title: Podcast: Georges St-Pierre, John Danaher & Gordon Ryan: The Greatest of All Time | Lex Fridman Podcast #260

body.input: rule sets. In the sport of grappling, if Gordon Ryan comes out and sits down in the middle

metadata.title: Podcast: Georges St-Pierre, John Danaher & Gordon Ryan: The Greatest of All Time | Lex Fridman Podcast #260

body.input: of the mat, his opponent must follow him to the ground and engage. In mixed martial arts,

metadata.title: Podcast: Georges St-Pierre, John Danaher & Gordon Ryan: The Greatest of All Time | Lex Fridman Podcast #260

body.input: if you come to the center of the cage and sit down, the other guy can just walk away

metadata.title: Podcast: Georges St-Pierre, John Danaher & Gordon Ryan: The Greatest of All Time | Lex Fridman Podcast #260

body.input: from you. They're completely oriented in different directions. Grappling is ground centered. MMA is

metadata.title: Podcast: Georges St-Pierre, John Danaher & Gordon Ryan: The Greatest of All Time | Lex Fridman Podcast #260

body.input: typically standing centered. At the beginning of every round, you have to start standing

metadata.title: Podcast: Georges St-Pierre, John Danaher & Gordon Ryan: The Greatest of All Time | Lex Fridman Podcast #260

body.input: again. If I disengage from a ground grappling situation, stand up and walk away from my

metadata.title: Podcast: Georges St-Pierre, John Danaher & Gordon Ryan: The Greatest of All Time | Lex Fridman Podcast #260

body.input: opponent, my opponent must follow me up to the feet. In grappling, it's the exact opposite.

metadata.title: Podcast: Georges St-Pierre, John Danaher & Gordon Ryan: The Greatest of All Time | Lex Fridman Podcast #260

body.input: If I sit to the ground, my opponent must follow me to the ground. It's written into the rule

metadata.title: Podcast: Georges St-Pierre, John Danaher & Gordon Ryan: The Greatest of All Time | Lex Fridman Podcast #260

body.input: set. And so one is inherently ground oriented and one is inherently standing oriented.

metadata.title: Podcast: Georges St-Pierre, John Danaher & Gordon Ryan: The Greatest of All Time | Lex Fridman Podcast #260

body.input: So it's more difficult to dictate where the fight happens in mixed martial arts.

metadata.title: Podcast: Georges St-Pierre, John Danaher & Gordon Ryan: The Greatest of All Time | Lex Fridman Podcast #260

body.input: Yes. You have to be able to impose where the fight happens.

metadata.title: Podcast: Georges St-Pierre, John Danaher & Gordon Ryan: The Greatest of All Time | Lex Fridman Podcast #260

body.input: You have to be able to impose where the fight is. Whereas in grappling, you can simply choose it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Georges St-Pierre, John Danaher & Gordon Ryan: The Greatest of All Time | Lex Fridman Podcast #260

body.input: So George, what is your sense of the difference in terms of how you approached it

metadata.title: Podcast: Georges St-Pierre, John Danaher & Gordon Ryan: The Greatest of All Time | Lex Fridman Podcast #260

body.input: between the two sports? You also are a student of wrestling and grappling. So in preparing for fights,

metadata.title: Podcast: Georges St-Pierre, John Danaher & Gordon Ryan: The Greatest of All Time | Lex Fridman Podcast #260

body.input: what parts of grappling, purely the sport that you have to leave behind?

metadata.title: Podcast: Georges St-Pierre, John Danaher & Gordon Ryan: The Greatest of All Time | Lex Fridman Podcast #260

body.input: Well, I'm very lucky. I had the opportunity to train with, I consider the best mentor,

metadata.title: Podcast: Georges St-Pierre, John Danaher & Gordon Ryan: The Greatest of All Time | Lex Fridman Podcast #260

body.input: trainer I ever had. And I have some of the best grapplers that I can train with. They were there

metadata.title: Podcast: Georges St-Pierre, John Danaher & Gordon Ryan: The Greatest of All Time | Lex Fridman Podcast #260

body.input: to help me through my career. So for my training is, of course, because I do not dedicate as much

metadata.title: Podcast: Georges St-Pierre, John Danaher & Gordon Ryan: The Greatest of All Time | Lex Fridman Podcast #260

body.input: time in one specific area, it's hard to be a world class athlete in only one particular area.

metadata.title: Podcast: Georges St-Pierre, John Danaher & Gordon Ryan: The Greatest of All Time | Lex Fridman Podcast #260

body.input: I always, for me, like the idea to be more well rounded, to be very competent in every of those

metadata.title: Podcast: Georges St-Pierre, John Danaher & Gordon Ryan: The Greatest of All Time | Lex Fridman Podcast #260

body.input: areas, striking, grappling, takedowns, and all those areas. Then being just very good at one

metadata.title: Podcast: Georges St-Pierre, John Danaher & Gordon Ryan: The Greatest of All Time | Lex Fridman Podcast #260

body.input: and not as good at others. Because I like the idea that it gives me more option when I fight someone,

metadata.title: Podcast: Georges St-Pierre, John Danaher & Gordon Ryan: The Greatest of All Time | Lex Fridman Podcast #260

body.input: I can mold myself to become the perfect nemesis to that person better if I'm more well rounded.

metadata.title: Podcast: Georges St-Pierre, John Danaher & Gordon Ryan: The Greatest of All Time | Lex Fridman Podcast #260

body.input: If I do not have those well rounded skill, I don't have that option.

metadata.title: Podcast: Georges St-Pierre, John Danaher & Gordon Ryan: The Greatest of All Time | Lex Fridman Podcast #260

body.input: You have less tools to work with, less technology. What about you, Gordon? What

metadata.title: Podcast: Georges St-Pierre, John Danaher & Gordon Ryan: The Greatest of All Time | Lex Fridman Podcast #260

body.input: do you think is very distinct about grappling and the way you approach it versus fighting?

metadata.title: Podcast: Georges St-Pierre, John Danaher & Gordon Ryan: The Greatest of All Time | Lex Fridman Podcast #260

body.input: I think most of it was covered. But I think that one of the big things is the fact that

metadata.title: Podcast: Georges St-Pierre, John Danaher & Gordon Ryan: The Greatest of All Time | Lex Fridman Podcast #260

body.input: when you're looking at MMA, you have a pretty general agreed upon and unified rule set. Where

metadata.title: Podcast: Georges St-Pierre, John Danaher & Gordon Ryan: The Greatest of All Time | Lex Fridman Podcast #260

body.input: if you look at UFC versus Bellator, they have slight differences in the rules maybe. But

metadata.title: Podcast: Georges St-Pierre, John Danaher & Gordon Ryan: The Greatest of All Time | Lex Fridman Podcast #260

body.input: it's pretty much the same thing. Whereas in grappling, you have EBI rules, then you have ADCC

metadata.title: Podcast: Georges St-Pierre, John Danaher & Gordon Ryan: The Greatest of All Time | Lex Fridman Podcast #260

body.input: rules, you have IBJJF rules, you have no time limit rules. And each rule set will play to the

metadata.title: Podcast: Georges St-Pierre, John Danaher & Gordon Ryan: The Greatest of All Time | Lex Fridman Podcast #260

body.input: skills of different athletes. If you do ADCC rules, it generally is slightly biased towards

metadata.title: Podcast: Georges St-Pierre, John Danaher & Gordon Ryan: The Greatest of All Time | Lex Fridman Podcast #260

body.input: wrestlers. Or if they can stall to the overtime and then hit a takedown in the overtime and not

metadata.title: Podcast: Georges St-Pierre, John Danaher & Gordon Ryan: The Greatest of All Time | Lex Fridman Podcast #260

body.input: really doing any jiu-jitsu, but they score a takedown, they're going to win. Whereas if you

metadata.title: Podcast: Georges St-Pierre, John Danaher & Gordon Ryan: The Greatest of All Time | Lex Fridman Podcast #260

body.input: have like an EBI, for example, you have to finish the guy in regulation or you start in a jiu-jitsu

metadata.title: Podcast: Georges St-Pierre, John Danaher & Gordon Ryan: The Greatest of All Time | Lex Fridman Podcast #260

body.input: position with your back taken or in an arm bar. So I think that you have certain rule sets that play

metadata.title: Podcast: Georges St-Pierre, John Danaher & Gordon Ryan: The Greatest of All Time | Lex Fridman Podcast #260

body.input: in the favor of certain athletes. And certain athletes can win in one rule set, but then they

metadata.title: Podcast: Georges St-Pierre, John Danaher & Gordon Ryan: The Greatest of All Time | Lex Fridman Podcast #260

body.input: just have no chance of winning in the other. Like when I fought Yuri the first time in EBI,

metadata.title: Podcast: Georges St-Pierre, John Danaher & Gordon Ryan: The Greatest of All Time | Lex Fridman Podcast #260

body.input: I beat him in EBI. The chances of me beating him on that night under an A-level rule set,

metadata.title: Podcast: Georges St-Pierre, John Danaher & Gordon Ryan: The Greatest of All Time | Lex Fridman Podcast #260

body.input: under an ADCC rule set were probably pretty low. When I fought Leandro Lowe under an ADCC rule set,

metadata.title: Podcast: Georges St-Pierre, John Danaher & Gordon Ryan: The Greatest of All Time | Lex Fridman Podcast #260

body.input: he beat me that day, but the chances of him beating me on the same day in an EBI rule set

metadata.title: Podcast: Georges St-Pierre, John Danaher & Gordon Ryan: The Greatest of All Time | Lex Fridman Podcast #260

body.input: were like next to zero. So I think it's interesting that in MMA, you have one unified rule set, which

metadata.title: Podcast: Georges St-Pierre, John Danaher & Gordon Ryan: The Greatest of All Time | Lex Fridman Podcast #260

body.input: have small differences, but they're all generally the same. And in jiu-jitsu, you have a wide variety

metadata.title: Podcast: Georges St-Pierre, John Danaher & Gordon Ryan: The Greatest of All Time | Lex Fridman Podcast #260

body.input: of different rule sets that have biases towards certain athletes' skill sets. You mentioned Leandro

metadata.title: Podcast: Georges St-Pierre, John Danaher & Gordon Ryan: The Greatest of All Time | Lex Fridman Podcast #260

body.input: Lowe. I got to ask you again about ADCC. You have lost very, very few times in your career.

metadata.title: Podcast: Georges St-Pierre, John Danaher & Gordon Ryan: The Greatest of All Time | Lex Fridman Podcast #260

body.input: One, I mean, the same is true for George. And the only person who has ever submitted you is Philippe

metadata.title: Podcast: Georges St-Pierre, John Danaher & Gordon Ryan: The Greatest of All Time | Lex Fridman Podcast #260

body.input: Peña. A black belt, yeah. A black belt. He is ADCC world champion, multiple time IBJJF,

metadata.title: Podcast: Georges St-Pierre, John Danaher & Gordon Ryan: The Greatest of All Time | Lex Fridman Podcast #260

body.input: Guianogi world champion. You may face him at ADCC or elsewhere in the future. Will you beat him?

metadata.title: Podcast: Georges St-Pierre, John Danaher & Gordon Ryan: The Greatest of All Time | Lex Fridman Podcast #260

body.input: Yes. I mean, I have to say yes, right? But I fought him initially when I first got my black belt,

metadata.title: Podcast: Georges St-Pierre, John Danaher & Gordon Ryan: The Greatest of All Time | Lex Fridman Podcast #260

body.input: then I fought him a year later, so 2016 and 2017. And despite what people remember about the match,

metadata.title: Podcast: Georges St-Pierre, John Danaher & Gordon Ryan: The Greatest of All Time | Lex Fridman Podcast #260

body.input: and whenever people talk about it, it's like, oh yeah, the guy who strangled Gordon. But no

metadata.title: Podcast: Georges St-Pierre, John Danaher & Gordon Ryan: The Greatest of All Time | Lex Fridman Podcast #260

body.input: one remembers that the first match was like a 45-minute war. And then the second match with the

metadata.title: Podcast: Georges St-Pierre, John Danaher & Gordon Ryan: The Greatest of All Time | Lex Fridman Podcast #260

body.input: full 20 minutes of ADCC. And if I didn't get my back taken in like the last minute and a half,

metadata.title: Podcast: Georges St-Pierre, John Danaher & Gordon Ryan: The Greatest of All Time | Lex Fridman Podcast #260

body.input: two minutes, it would have went into an overtime. And that could have changed the outcome of the

metadata.title: Podcast: Georges St-Pierre, John Danaher & Gordon Ryan: The Greatest of All Time | Lex Fridman Podcast #260

body.input: match. I think that if you look at Philippe's performances, especially Nogi, specifically Nogi

metadata.title: Podcast: Georges St-Pierre, John Danaher & Gordon Ryan: The Greatest of All Time | Lex Fridman Podcast #260

body.input: since then, it looks like he's almost gotten worse. Whereas since that match in 2017,

metadata.title: Podcast: Georges St-Pierre, John Danaher & Gordon Ryan: The Greatest of All Time | Lex Fridman Podcast #260

body.input: the only match I lost after that was against Vinny Magalache by points. And I'm on like a 55-match

metadata.title: Podcast: Georges St-Pierre, John Danaher & Gordon Ryan: The Greatest of All Time | Lex Fridman Podcast #260

body.input: win streak over the course of four years, winning all the major tournaments Nogi. And Philippe,

metadata.title: Podcast: Georges St-Pierre, John Danaher & Gordon Ryan: The Greatest of All Time | Lex Fridman Podcast #260

body.input: since that match, I think is like five and two Nogi. And he's lost his last two matches. One

metadata.title: Podcast: Georges St-Pierre, John Danaher & Gordon Ryan: The Greatest of All Time | Lex Fridman Podcast #260

body.input: was convincingly where he was dominated by Andre and one was by submission. So I don't think that

metadata.title: Podcast: Georges St-Pierre, John Danaher & Gordon Ryan: The Greatest of All Time | Lex Fridman Podcast #260

body.input: he's progressed nearly as fast. If anything, he looks like he's worse than he was when he beat me

metadata.title: Podcast: Georges St-Pierre, John Danaher & Gordon Ryan: The Greatest of All Time | Lex Fridman Podcast #260

body.input: in 2017 based on his previous performances. That being said, I know he's going to come in training

metadata.title: Podcast: Georges St-Pierre, John Danaher & Gordon Ryan: The Greatest of All Time | Lex Fridman Podcast #260

body.input: very hard for this one and he's going to be prepared. But I just don't think that in terms

metadata.title: Podcast: Georges St-Pierre, John Danaher & Gordon Ryan: The Greatest of All Time | Lex Fridman Podcast #260

body.input: of technical ability, he's anywhere near my level. And he was much bigger than me both times we fought.

metadata.title: Podcast: Georges St-Pierre, John Danaher & Gordon Ryan: The Greatest of All Time | Lex Fridman Podcast #260

body.input: The first time he was much bigger than me. The second time he was one way class above me.

metadata.title: Podcast: Georges St-Pierre, John Danaher & Gordon Ryan: The Greatest of All Time | Lex Fridman Podcast #260

body.input: So now there's not going to be an advantage in technicality and there's also not going to be a

metadata.title: Podcast: Georges St-Pierre, John Danaher & Gordon Ryan: The Greatest of All Time | Lex Fridman Podcast #260

body.input: physicality advantage. So I think he's just going to be beat everywhere.

metadata.title: Podcast: Georges St-Pierre, John Danaher & Gordon Ryan: The Greatest of All Time | Lex Fridman Podcast #260

body.input: This is a good example of the scientific response to a comment, to a question. Yeah, so he's not,

metadata.title: Podcast: Georges St-Pierre, John Danaher & Gordon Ryan: The Greatest of All Time | Lex Fridman Podcast #260

body.input: that's a match you're not deeply concerned with in terms of the set of opponents because you have

metadata.title: Podcast: Georges St-Pierre, John Danaher & Gordon Ryan: The Greatest of All Time | Lex Fridman Podcast #260

body.input: and you will be facing a lot of really difficult. That's actually, in my opinion, one of the easier

body.input: matches because of the fact that we're relatively the same size. And I think that's the biggest

metadata.title: Podcast: Georges St-Pierre, John Danaher & Gordon Ryan: The Greatest of All Time | Lex Fridman Podcast #260

body.input: difference. If I show up at 230 pounds, like a lot of the guys are 260, 270 plus. So that extra weight

metadata.title: Podcast: Georges St-Pierre, John Danaher & Gordon Ryan: The Greatest of All Time | Lex Fridman Podcast #260

body.input: doesn't make a difference. I think out of that entire bracket, Felipe is probably going to be

metadata.title: Podcast: Georges St-Pierre, John Danaher & Gordon Ryan: The Greatest of All Time | Lex Fridman Podcast #260

metadata.title: Podcast: Georges St-Pierre, John Danaher & Gordon Ryan: The Greatest of All Time | Lex Fridman Podcast #260

body.input: them. And I think it may be, they may be longer drawn out matches because of the fact that they're

metadata.title: Podcast: Georges St-Pierre, John Danaher & Gordon Ryan: The Greatest of All Time | Lex Fridman Podcast #260

metadata.title: Podcast: Georges St-Pierre, John Danaher & Gordon Ryan: The Greatest of All Time | Lex Fridman Podcast #260

metadata.title: Podcast: Georges St-Pierre, John Danaher & Gordon Ryan: The Greatest of All Time | Lex Fridman Podcast #260

metadata.title: Podcast: Georges St-Pierre, John Danaher & Gordon Ryan: The Greatest of All Time | Lex Fridman Podcast #260
